en: The Sutra Spoken by the Buddha on the Original Deeds of the Bodhisattva, Volume One.
The translator’s name is lost; it is now appended to the records of the Eastern Jin dynasty.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the Garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. At that time...
At that time, the World-Honored One, seeing that the śramaṇas were indolent in body and mind and lacked diligent effort, addressed Ānanda, saying:
"Indolence is a burden to all practices. If those living at home are indolent, they will lack sufficient food and clothing, and their livelihoods will not flourish;
if those who have left the home life are indolent, they will be unable to escape the suffering of birth and death."

All matters are brought about through diligence; for those in the household life, diligence results in an abundance of food and clothing and the expansion of their livelihoods, such that they are praised from near and far;
for those who have left the household life, diligence ensures that the practice of the Path is fully accomplished.

If you wish to attain the fulfillment of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, the treasury of all dhyānas, samādhis, and the dharmas of the Path, and to cut off the stream of birth and death to reach the shore of nirvāṇa—the unconditioned peace and bliss—you must take diligent effort and arduous cultivation as your foundation.

If one wishes to attain the six perfections (ṣaṭ-pāramitā), the four immeasurables (catvāry apramāṇāni), the four debts of gratitude, the ten powers (daśa-balāni) of a Tathāgata, the four fearlessnesses (catvāri vaiśāradyāni), the eighteen unique qualities (āveṇika-dharmāḥ), the six supernormal knowledges (ṣaḍ-abhijñāḥ), the three types of penetration, and the realization of all-knowledge (sarvajñatā);

or if one wishes to be fully endowed with the thirty-two marks (dvātriṃśan-mahāpuruṣalakṣaṇāni) and the eighty minor characteristics (aśīty-anuvyañjanāni), to adorn and purify buddha-fields, and to teach and transform sentient beings— all these are accomplished through diligence (vīrya).
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"In the past, incalculable eons ago, there were five hundred sons of elders who established a great sacrificial altar, raised a great banner, and beat drums to proclaim:
'To śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, and the poor who beg, I shall give all things as alms.'"
The five hundred sons of the elders each brought forth precious jewels, elephants, horses, carriages, clothing, and food and drink, giving them all according to whatever each lacked.

At that time, there was a poor man who, having traveled through various kingdoms, arrived in this country. He saw five hundred sons of elders establishing a great altar to bestow gifts, relieving the destitute, aiding the needy, and rescuing all beings without any sense of regret or withholding. He asked them, saying:
"For what kind of vow do you seek to perform these meritorious acts of giving?"
He then replied, "I wish to seek the path of Buddhahood with these merits.
At that time, the poor man asked again:
"What is called the Buddha-way, and what are its teachings?
The sons of the elders replied to him, saying:

"As for the Buddha-way, it surpasses that of the Arhats and Pratyekabuddhas; it is uniquely honored within the three realms, the teacher of gods and humans, possessing immeasurable great kindness and infinite great compassion. It universally pities the various classes of beings in the five destinies as if they were its own infants, teaching and transforming all so that they may practice goodness, severing the sufferings of the three miserable realms for sentient beings and delivering them across the sea of birth and death to reach the place of Nirvana and peace."

What is called a Buddha is one for whom all evils have been forever exhausted and all virtues universally assembled; who is free from further defilements and in whom all desires are utterly extinguished; whose six perfections (ṣaṭ-pāramitā) are completely fulfilled; who, through skillful means (upāya-kauśalya), teaches and transforms beings according to the time without limit; who possesses the ten powers (daśa-bala), the four fearlessnesses (catvāri vaiśāradyāni), and the eighteen unique and extraordinary dharmas (āveṇika-dharmāḥ); and who possesses the inexhaustible treasury of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (saptatriṃśad-bodhipakṣa-dharmāḥ).
His body was the color of purple-gold, endowed with the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics; his six supernormal powers were pure and penetrating, free from all obstruction.

He knew the infinite past and beheld the boundless future; there was nothing among present affairs he did not know. His threefold penetration and far-reaching insight were manifested through the ten powers.
"Because he possesses such virtues, he is titled 'Buddha.
Each of the sons of the elders likewise praised the Buddha’s immeasurable virtuous conduct in this very manner.
At that time, having heard of the Buddha’s merits, the poor man thought to himself:
"I too now wish to study this vow to universally deliver all beings;
yet, being destitute and possessing no wealth or treasures, with what shall I practice giving?"
He thought to himself:
"I shall offer my own body as a gift.
Having formed this thought, he went out to seek honey with which to smear his body, and then lay down among the graves.
He then made this vow:
"I now give my body as an offering to all beings; if there be those who require my flesh, head, eyes, marrow, or brain, I shall give them all.
By means of this merit, I seek the path of the Buddha to universally deliver all beings."
"Having made this vow, at that moment the trichiliocosm shook violently, and the palaces of the devas surged and subsided in towering waves.
Then, the devas and humans were thrown into a state of frantic agitation and terror."

Śakra Devānām-Indra immediately observed Jambudvīpa with his divine eye and saw that the Bodhisattva was in a cemetery, giving his body as alms. He then descended to test him, transforming himself into various dogs, birds, and wild beasts, intending to come and devour him.
Thereupon, when the Bodhisattva saw the various dogs and birds coming to devour his body, his mind was filled with joy, and he felt no sense of retreat, wavering, or agitation.
At that time, Śakra, Lord of Devas, resumed his celestial form and praised him, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!
How truly marvelous and unsurpassed!"
"What aspiration do you seek through the merit you have performed?
Is it the position of a Heavenly Lord, a Brahmā King, or a Wheel-Turning King?
Thereupon, the Bodhisattva rose and replied:

"I do not seek the status of a celestial lord, a wheel-turning sage king, a Mara king, or a Brahma king; nor do I aspire to the pleasures of the three realms. Now, with my utmost sincerity, I desire to seek the Buddha-way."
Since I am poor and possess no wealth or treasures with which to practice giving, I offer my own body as a gift to seek the Buddha-way and extensively deliver all immeasurable sentient beings.
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, and countless other devas praised him with one voice, saying:
“Excellent, excellent!
How extraordinary and unsurpassed!”
Then, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, spoke these verses:
"Those who seek the most supreme path do not begrudge their own bodies or lives;
they cast away their bodies like refuse or soil, having realized that there is no self."
"Though one gives away wealth and treasures, this matter is not difficult;
for one who is thus courageous, through such diligence, Buddhahood will be swiftly attained.
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, spoke to the Bodhisattva, saying:

“Your great courage and diligence are difficult to equal; they surpass the offerings made by these five hundred bodhisattvas by hundreds of thousands of billions of times, even beyond measure. You shall be the first to attain Buddhahood.”
Śakra and the various devas scattered celestial fragrant flowers upon him and departed with joy.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"The poor man at that time was my very self."
The five hundred sons of elders are these very five hundred bodhisattvas, Maitreya and the others.
Because of my diligence and valor, I have surpassed the meritorious deeds performed by all these bodhisattvas and attained Buddhahood first; one must not fail to pursue diligent and arduous practice.
“Such is the giving of a bodhisattva.

Thereupon, Ānanda and the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, were all filled with joy; they paid homage to the Buddha and each applied themselves with diligence to cultivate the practices of the Path.
Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

There was a householder of immeasurable wealth whose precious treasures exceeded those in the royal treasury; his name was Mahānāman. He was stingy and greedy by nature, not daring to eat or wear fine things himself, and he did not know how to practice giving.

When he goes out, he rides in a dilapidated old cart with a thatch roof made of woven grass; he wears tattered, worn-out clothes and eats only stale, moldy grain, never fine food, and as soon as he has eaten, he closes his door.

At that time, his illness became so grave that he passed away; furthermore, as he had no offspring, King Prasenajit confiscated all his wealth and treasures, leaving neither his own person nor his wife and daughters to enjoy its benefits.
King Prasenajit went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, withdrew to his usual seat, and asked the World-Honored One:

"In my kingdom there was a householder named Mahānāman who was stingy and greedy; he was unwilling to practice giving and did not know how to provide for food and clothing. He has now died; in which realm has he been reborn?"
The Buddha told the king:
"He shall fall into the Lohakṣa (Iron Heat) Hell, where he will undergo manifold sufferings for many tens of millions of years.

Upon emerging from that hell, he shall fall among the hungry ghosts (preta), suffering from hunger and thirst day and night with his body constantly ablaze; for hundreds of thousands of millions of years, he shall never even hear the names of water or grain."
Upon hearing the Buddha’s words, the king’s heart was struck with alarm and his hair stood on end; he wept with such grief and choked sobs that he could not restrain himself.
The Buddha said to the king:
“One who is wise is able to abandon stinginess and greed to practice giving; such a person obtains protection in the present life and receives blessings in future lives.”

In a past age, in this Jambudvīpa, there was a great king named Kanakavarmā. He was compassionate and benevolent by nature and ruled over eighty-four thousand minor kings throughout Jambudvīpa. He had ten thousand ministers, twenty thousand court ladies, and ten thousand queens, and his subjects were prosperous and flourishing.
At that time, the planet Mars appeared in its course; the court astrologer divined it and declared that there would be a drought lasting twelve years.
The astrologer informed the king:
"The movement of the stars has manifested a change; for twelve years throughout Jambudvīpa, there shall be a drought with no rain."
"If it does not rain, the five grains will not be harvested; the people will suffer from hunger and the land will fall into great desolation. What should we do?

When the king heard this, he was deeply distressed and immediately commanded his ministers to summon eighty-four thousand minor kings to assemble. They were all ordered to record the number of inhabitants and to list the current quantity of grain in pecks and bushels. Without distinction of male or female, noble or humble, rich or poor, old or young, they were to calculate the population and the days; each person was to be given one *sheng* of millet per day, and no more could be eaten.

The ministers and all the kings received these instructions and each returned to his own kingdom, issuing proclamations throughout their respective jurisdictions that everything was to be done accordingly.

From that time forward, there was no rain and the heavens remained parched; there was neither plowing nor sowing, and no rice or grain remained. The people suffered from famine, and those who died were exceedingly numerous.
The ministers addressed the king, saying, "The people are starving and distressed; those who have died are exceedingly numerous.

The king commanded his ministers to issue a proclamation throughout all the kingdoms, instructing the people that each should observe the ten wholesome actions (*daśakuśala*). He declared, "Though their bodies perish, their spirits shall attain birth in heaven, where happiness is spontaneous."
The ministers, having received these instructions, each issued proclamations:
"All people, great and small, shall observe the ten wholesome precepts; those who die shall all be reborn in the heavens.

At that time, there was a man of exceptional intelligence and wisdom, whose physical appearance was peerless. He saw the mother of a neighbor engaging in illicit relations with her son; upon seeing this, his heart became distressed, and he thought to himself:

"Though one has obtained a human body, one acts like a beast, deluded by form and desire; the child does not recognize the mother, nor does the mother recognize the child. With topsy-turvy relations and no mutual discernment, the cycle of birth and death is truly and most dreadfully terrifying."
He immediately shaved his head, donned the kāṣāya robe, and went to the mountains and marshes to practice dhyāna and contemplate:
"It is because of ignorance, greed, lust, and hatred that various formations arise; thus one undergoes the manifold sufferings of birth and death within the five realms of existence."

"If there are no three poisons, then there are no volitional formations (*saṃskāra*); when volitional formations have ceased, one does not receive a body; once the body no longer exists, all sufferings are extinguished.
Contemplating in this way, his mind suddenly attained liberation, and all desires were forever exhausted.
Immediately, he attained the path of a pratyekabuddha; his six supernormal powers were clear and penetrating, free from all obstruction.
He then thought to himself: "Whose food should I now receive?"
"Observing all the people of Jambudvīpa, they are all starving and food cannot be obtained; I can only go to where the Great King Kanakavarmā is to beg for alms."
Even if he flew into the Great King’s palace to beg for food, the king would say:
"My meal is limited to this; it is finished today."
The king thought to himself:
"Now, even as I eat, I shall eventually die;
yet if I do not eat..."
"I too shall surely die.
Now that I have encountered this divine being, so difficult to meet, I would rather go without food myself than fail to offer a meal to this noble person.
Having said this, he took his own portion of food and immediately offered it to this Pratyekabuddha.
After the Pratyekabuddha had finished eating the meal, he thought to himself:
"The generosity bestowed by this Great King is difficult to equal; I shall cause the King to feel even greater joy."

Immediately before the King, he ascended into the void and manifested transformations, leaping up in the east and sinking in the west, leaping up in the west and sinking in the east, leaping up in the south and sinking in the north, leaping up in the north and sinking in the south, leaping up above and sinking below, and leaping up below and sinking above. He walked upon the void, sometimes sitting and sometimes lying down; water issued from the upper part of his body while fire issued from the lower part, and water issued from the lower part of his body while fire issued from the upper part. He divided his single body into a hundred, a thousand, ten thousand, and even into countless bodies, and then merged those countless bodies back into one.
Having finished manifesting these transformations, he descended from the sky and stood before the king, saying to him:
"The gift you have now bestowed is truly beyond compare; whatever boon you seek, I shall surely grant it to you."

The king, along with his ministers, ladies, and court maids, were all filled with great joy. They prostrated themselves, touching their heads to the ground to pay homage at the feet of the Pratyekabuddha, and made this aspiration:

"Now the people of our kingdom are suffering from famine; their distress is extreme and their lives hang by a thread. We now offer these last remaining morsels of food to this noble being (Mahāsattva). By means of this merit, may we eliminate the hunger and distress within our land; this alone is the boon we seek."
Then the Pratyekabuddha replied to the king, saying,
"It shall be as you wish.
Having finished speaking, he immediately flew away.

"At that moment, clouds arose from the four directions and merged with the void; a great wind then blew away the impurities of the earth, clearing away all filth and excrement so they were transformed and vanished. Then, food and drink of a hundred natural flavors rained down, pervading all of Jambudvīpa."

Again, there fell a rain of the five grains; next, a rain of garments; and finally, a rain of the seven treasures. Within Jambudvīpa, the eighty-four thousand kings, ministers, and subjects were all filled with great joy.
The King issued a decree to his ministers and proclaimed to the eighty-four thousand kings:
"Each of you must command your respective jurisdictions so that all the people shall uphold the ten wholesome actions.

At that time, the five grains flourished throughout Jambudvīpa; the people rejoiced as they practiced the ten wholesome actions, regarding one another with kindness as they would a father, a mother, an elder brother, or a younger brother.
At that time, after the people’s lives ended, they were all reborn in the heavens, and none fell into the three evil realms.
The Buddha told the king: “At that time, Kanakavarmī was my own self.”
At that time, by simply offering a single meal to a Pratyekabuddha, I obtained such merit and blessings in this present life.

By virtue of this merit, I have personally attained Buddhahood; may all sentient beings who suffer from hunger and thirst obtain the realization of the Way, and may they find peace, security, and joy, reaching the state of the Unconditioned.
At that time, all the disciples, kings, ministers, and citizens were filled with great joy.
Then, the World-Honored One addressed the king again, saying:
"All sentient beings are bound by stinginess and grasping, and shrouded by the veil of avarice; they do not know that through practicing giving, one obtains a great reward that is beyond measure."
He reflected: "In a past life long ago, in this Jambudvīpa, there was a city named Anavataṃsā; the king’s name was Bandhuma, and his queen’s name was Bhadrā."
At that time, grain was expensive and the people were suffering from famine, compounded by a plague.

The king himself was also ill, so the queen went out in person to sacrifice to the heavens. Along the roadside there was a certain household; the husband was away on a journey when his wife gave birth to a child. Having no maidservants and being exhausted from childbirth, she had no food and was starving to death.
She thought to herself: "Death is now imminent and there is no other recourse; I must simply eat my own child to sustain my life."
She immediately took up a knife, intending to kill her son; moved by deep compassion, she raised her voice and wept aloud.
At that time, the lady was about to return to the palace, but hearing this woman’s piteous and piercing cries, she was struck with sorrow and pity, and stopped to listen.
Just as this woman was about to raise her knife to kill her son, she thought to herself:
"How can I bear to eat my own son's flesh?
Having had this thought, she immediately began to weep.
The lady then entered his house, approached him, and asked:
"Why are you weeping? What do you intend to do?"
The wife immediately replied:
"I have no food to eat; moreover, having recently given birth, my body is doubly weak and emaciated. I wish to kill my child in order to save my own life."
Upon hearing this, the lady was filled with sorrow and compassion, and she said:
"Do not kill her son!
I shall go to the palace and bring food for him."
The woman replied, "The noble lady is of high station;
she may perhaps delay or even forget [this matter]. But today my life hangs by a thread and will not last beyond this moment. It would be better for me to eat my own son to sustain my life."
The lady asked, "Would it be acceptable to obtain other meat to eat? He replied:
"Even if it results in saving my life, I do not ask whether it is beautiful or ugly.
Thereupon, the lady immediately took a knife and cut off her own breast, making this vow:

"Now I offer this breast as a gift to relieve this perilous distress; I do not wish to become a Wheel-Turning Sage King, a Heavenly Lord, a Demon King, or a Brahma King. I shall take this merit to accomplish the unsurpassed, true, and correct Way."
He then took the milk and gave it to this woman.
Just as he was about to raise his knife to cut off another breast, at that very moment the great trichiliocosm shook violently, and all the celestial palaces trembled.
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, beheld her with his divine eye as the lady cut her own breast to relieve her perilous distress.
Thereupon, Śakra and countless devas immediately descended and remained suspended in the air, all weeping with tears falling like heavy rain.
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, stood before the lady and asked:
"The gift you have now bestowed is most difficult to equal;
what vow do you seek? The lady replied:
"By employing these merits, I seek the unsurpassed, truly correct path to deliver all sentient beings from suffering and calamity.
The Heavenly Emperor replied,
"What proof do you have for seeking this vow?"
Thereupon, the lady immediately made this vow:
"If the merit of my gift is truly destined for the attainment of perfect enlightenment, may my breasts be restored to their former state at once."
At that moment, her breast was restored to its former state.
The Heavenly Emperor praised her, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!"
"You shall attain Buddhahood before long.
The devas were filled with joy; they immediately manifested their forms and praised the lady, saying:
"Do you feel no regret for the gift you have now bestowed?"
"Do you consider it painful? He replied,
"I have no regret, nor do I consider it painful."
The deity replied again:
"If you have no regrets, what can serve as proof?
Thereupon, the lady made this solemn vow:
"I now offer this gift in my quest for the Buddha-way; may I, being free from regret, have this female body transformed into that of a man.
As soon as she had finished making this vow, her female body was instantly transformed into that of a man.
At that time, the devas praised him, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!
Just as you have vowed, you shall attain Buddhahood before long."

The king, his ministers, and the common people marveled at this as most extraordinary and rejoiced immeasurably. At that time, all manner of diseases within the kingdom were eliminated; grain became abundant and cheap, and the people lived in peace and happiness.
"After some time, when the king passes away, the ministers will deliberate together on who should be established as the new king.
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, will descend and say to the ministers:
'Varmakṣatriya has transformed his body into that of a man; furthermore, he possesses merit and virtue, and thus he ought to become king.'"
The ministers rejoiced and immediately prostrated themselves, crowning him as king; the population flourished and the kingdom subsequently prospered.
The Buddha said to the king:
"He who was Varmakhaṭi at that time is my very self now."
At that time, I did not spare my own body or life as I practiced such giving;
I received the reward in this very life, whereby my body was transformed into that of a man and I succeeded to the throne.
"By virtue of these merits, he has now attained Buddhahood to universally save all beings.
The Bodhisattva’s practice of the *dānapāramitā* is thus courageous and fierce.
All the disciples, kings, ministers, and subjects were filled with great joy; they prostrated themselves before the Buddha and departed.
Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

In that city there was a brahmin who had established a sacrificial altar outside the city and prepared food and drink; having invited various brahmins and completed the sacrifice, he then returned to the city.

At that time, as the Buddha entered the city to beg for alms, he came out onto the road and beheld the Buddha’s majestic and towering radiance; filled with joy and leaping for gladness, he circumambulated the Buddha once, paid his respects, and departed.

At that time, the Buddha smiled, and light issued from his mouth, illuminating the ten directions. It reached upward as far as the Heaven of the Thirty-three and downward as far as the great hells, including all animals, birds, and beasts, as well as the various hungry ghosts; there was no realm within the five paths of existence that did not receive this radiance. Those who were ill were all healed, and those imprisoned and confined in jails were all released and set free.

When the devas and humans beheld the Buddha’s radiance, they were filled with immeasurable joy and came before the Buddha, offering various flowers and incense as an offering to the World-Honored One.
Ānanda knelt down on his right knee and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Today the World-Honored One has smiled in such a manner; I pray that you will explain the meaning of this smile.”
The Buddha said to Ānanda,
“Do you see this brahmin who has circumambulated the Buddha once? He replied:
“Yes, I saw him. The Buddha told Ānanda:
“This brahmin, seeing the Buddha with joy, paid pure and respectful homage by circumambulating the Buddha once.”
By this merit, from this time forward for twenty-five kalpas he shall not fall into the three miserable realms; wherever he is born among devas or humans, his happiness shall be boundless.
At the end of those twenty-five kalpas, he shall attain the state of a Pratyekabuddha, named Tṛṃśa-kīrti.

When Ānanda and the entire great assembly heard what the Buddha had spoken, their bodies and minds were purified; some attained the stage of Srotāpanna, Sakṛdāgāmin, Anāgāmin, or Arhat, while others resolved to attain the unsurpassed, right, and true path.
The assembly rejoiced, prostrated before the Buddha, circumambulated him to the right, and departed.
Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying in the kingdom of Uttarakuru, together with one thousand two hundred and fifty śramaṇas, as they traveled toward a village.

The Tathāgata possesses thirty-two marks of physical excellence and eighty secondary characteristics; his radiance is so brilliant that it illuminates heaven and earth, leaving nothing in great darkness.
He is like the full moon, which shines with particular brilliance among the stars.
At that time, the weather was intensely hot and there was no shade or coolness. There was a shepherd who, seeing the Buddha’s radiant marks, thought to himself:
"The Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, the Teacher of the Three Realms, is traversing this intense heat without any shade or coolness."
He immediately wove grass into a canopy to cover the Buddha above him and followed behind the Buddha as he walked.
When they had gone quite far from the sheep, he released the canopy, let it fall to the ground, and returned toward the side of the sheep.

The Buddha then smiled, and from his mouth issued golden light in tens of millions of branches; from each branch emerged hundreds of thousands of millions of rays, illuminating the ten directions. Reaching upward to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven and downward to the eighteen hells, no creature—be they birds, beasts, or hungry ghosts—was not bathed in great brilliance.

When the devas and humans of the three realms beheld the Buddha’s radiance, they all came to the Buddha’s presence at that very moment. All the people, as well as the various nāgas and asuras—this vast assembly of countless beings—were filled with great joy and offered incense, flowers, and music to the Tathāgata.
Ānanda knelt down with his right knee on the ground and addressed the Buddha, saying, “The Buddha does not smile without cause; I pray that you will explain its meaning.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"Do you see this shepherd now? He replied, "Indeed, I see him."
The Buddha told Ānanda:

“Because this cowherd, with a heart of reverence, used a grass canopy to cover the Buddha, by virtue of this merit, for thirteen kalpas he was born in places of high honor among gods and humans; there was always a canopy of the seven treasures spontaneously appearing above him.”
After his life ended, he did not fall into the three evil realms.
Having practiced the Way as a renunciant for thirteen kalpas, he became a pratyekabuddha named Anupada.

When the entire great assembly heard what the Buddha had spoken, some attained the realization of the stage of stream-entry, once-returning, non-returning, or arhatship; some became pratyekabuddhas; some resolved their minds upon unsurpassed, perfect, and true enlightenment; and some established themselves on the stage of non-retrogression.
The assembly rejoiced, paid homage to the Buddha, and departed.
Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

The Buddha’s honored disciple named Śāriputra constantly observed sentient beings with his Dharma-eye throughout the six periods of the day and night; whenever there were those who should be delivered, he would immediately go to deliver them.
King Prasenajit had a high minister named Śreṣṭhin, whose wealth was immeasurable; he was ready to attain deliverance at that time.
Then, on the following morning, Śāriputra dressed in his robes, took up his alms bowl, and went to his house to beg for food.
Thereupon, the teacher Śreṇika saw him, immediately paid homage, inquired after his well-being, and invited him to enter and sit; he then provided him with a seat and offered him food.
When Śāriputra had finished eating, washed his hands, and rinsed his mouth, he preached the Dharma for him, saying:

"Wealth, nobility, and honor are the root of all suffering. The affection of household life is like being within a prison. All that exists is impermanent. The honors of the three realms are like illusions and transformations. Within the cycle of birth and death in the five destinies, one merely changes physical forms; there is no 'self' to be found."

Upon hearing the Dharma, the Master’s mind was struck with awe; he no longer aspired to honor or wealth, nor did he delight in affection or kinship. He viewed his home life as nothing more than a burial mound, and consequently entrusted all his household affairs and property to his younger brother. He then shaved his hair and beard, donned the *kāṣāya*, and entered the deep mountains to practice meditation and cultivate the Way.
His wife was filled with sorrow and anxiety; she longed for her former husband and could not comply with her current husband.
Her husband asked her, "Our household possesses much wealth, property, and precious jewels; what is lacking that you are constantly sad and unhappy?"
His wife replied, "I am grieving because I am thinking of my former husband.
Her husband asked again:
"You have now become my husband and wife; why do you think of your former husband day and night?
The woman replied again, "My former husband’s heart and mind were incomparably good; that is why I think of him."
When the younger brother saw his sister-in-law’s longing [for her husband], he feared that once her brother returned and renounced his worldly life, he would reclaim their property;
he then said to the leader of the bandits, “I will pay you five hundred gold coins to cut off that śramaṇa’s head and bring it here.”
The bandit leader accepted the money and went into the mountains to see that śramaṇa.
The śramaṇa said to him, "I have only tattered robes and no possessions; why have you come?"
The bandit immediately replied,
"Your younger brother hired me to come and kill you.
Terrified, the śramaṇa then said to the bandit:
"I am but a newly ordained practitioner of the Way; furthermore, I have not yet seen the Buddha and do not understand the Dharma. Please do not kill me!
I must wait until I have seen the Buddha and gained some understanding of the sutras and teachings; it will not be too late to kill me then."
The bandits said to him, "We must kill you now; we will not stop.
The śramaṇa then raised one arm and spoke to the bandits, saying:
“Cut off one arm and spare my remaining life so that I may see the Buddha.
Thereupon, the bandit cut off an arm and took it away to give to his younger brother.
Then the śramaṇa went to see the Buddha; having paid homage, he sat to one side, and the Buddha preached the Dharma for him:

"Throughout countless kalpas in the distant past, the blood from your severed heads, hands, and feet has exceeded the waters of the four great oceans; the bones accumulated from your bodies would tower higher than Mount Sumeru; the tears shed in weeping have surpassed the four seas; and the milk you drank from your kin exceeds the volume of rivers and oceans—not only in this present life, but from countless kalpas ago."

All who possess a body undergo manifold sufferings; all manifold sufferings arise from habitual practice. Because of the habituation of craving, these manifold sufferings exist; once delusion and craving are severed, one no longer practices various activities. When one no longer practices various activities, the body ceases to exist; when the body no longer exists, manifold sufferings are extinguished. One should therefore contemplate only the Eightfold Noble Path.

Thereupon, upon hearing what the Buddha had spoken, the śramaṇa’s mind was suddenly and clearly liberated; he immediately attained the path of arhatship before the Buddha and, relinquishing his life-force, entered parinirvāṇa.

The thief took his arm and went to give it to his younger brother; the brother then placed the arm before his sister-in-law and said to her, "She always says she longs for her former husband; this is his arm."
His sister-in-law wept with a choked voice in grief and went to inform the king.
The king immediately investigated and found it to be true and not false;
he then executed his younger brother.
The bhikṣus had doubts and asked the Buddha:
"What evil deeds did this śramaṇa commit in his previous lives that he now has his arm cut off?
What roots of virtue did he cultivate that he now encounters the World-Honored One and attains the path of Arhatship?"
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"In the distant past, in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī, there was a king named Brahmadatta. Once, while out hunting and pursuing wild beasts, he lost his way and could not find the path back."
The trees and grasses reached toward the heavens, and there was no other means by which he could escape; seized by great terror, he continued forward until he saw a Pratyekabuddha.
The king asked him, saying:
"Having lost my way, by what means can I emerge?
Where are the army, the horses, and the multitude of people?"
At that time, the Pratyekabuddha had a malignant ulcer on his arm and was unable to raise it; he therefore held up his foot to show him the path.
The king then became enraged and said:
"This man is my subject; seeing me, he did not rise, but instead holds up his foot to show me the way?"
The king then drew his sword and severed his arm.
At that time, the Pratyekabuddha thought to himself:
"If the king does not repent and reproach himself for his past actions, he shall suffer heavy retribution with no prospect of escape."
Thereupon, the Pratyekabuddha immediately ascended into the void before the king, manifesting his supernormal powers.
Seeing this, the king cast himself upon the ground, wailing aloud and repenting his transgressions with self-reproach: "Pratyekabuddha!"
"I only pray that you will descend and accept my repentance.
At that time, the Pratyekabuddha immediately descended and accepted his repentance.
The king placed his head at the feet of the Pratyekabuddha, paid homage, and spoke thus:
"Please have compassion for me and accept my repentance; I pray that you will not cause me to suffer pain for long.
At that time, the Pratyekabuddha relinquished his life-force and entered *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*.
The king then collected the relics, erected a stupa, and made offerings of flowers and incense; by constantly repenting and making vows before the stupa, he attained liberation.
The Buddha said, "The king at that time was this very śramaṇa."
Because he severed the arm of a pratyekabuddha, for five hundred lifetimes he was constantly killed by having his arm severed, continuing until this present day.
Due to his repentance, however, he did not fall into hell; through the wisdom of understanding, he attained liberation and realized the path of an arhat.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
“All calamities and blessings ultimately never perish.
Upon hearing what the Buddha had said, the bhikṣus were all struck with awe and alarm; they prostrated themselves, touching their heads to the ground in salutation.
In the past, when the Buddha was at Lake Anavatapta, he addressed five hundred arhats, saying:
"Each of you should speak individually of your past deeds in previous lives by which you have now attained the Way."
At that time, the Arhats, having received the Buddha’s instructions, each spoke of the merits they had cultivated through their past deeds. Then, an Arhat named Pāṭakāli spoke of himself:

"Innumerable kalpas ago, there was a Buddha in the world named Dīpaṃkara Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Perfect in Knowledge and Conduct, Sugata, Knower of the World, Unsurpassed One, Tamer of Men, Teacher of Gods and Humans. Possessing great compassion, he was a benefactor to all; he arose in the world as a great refuge for sentient beings, teaching and transforming gods and humans so that they all attained the Way, and then entered parinirvāṇa, after which his relics were distributed and stūpas and temples were erected."

At the time when the Dharma is about to perish, I was a poor man; having no other means of livelihood and driven by desperation, I went out to gather firewood. From afar, I saw within a vast marsh a stupa-temple that was most magnificent and towering.

At that time, upon seeing this, my heart was filled with immeasurable joy and exultation; I immediately went to the site of the stupa, and beholding the image therein, I paid homage with great delight.

He saw foxes, wolves, birds, and wild beasts dwelling within it; grasses, trees, thorns, and brambles filled it with impurity; it was utterly desolate and devoid of people, with no tracks of human passage and no one to offer worship.

Yet as I beheld this activity of the mind, I felt deep sorrow; not understanding the Dharma of the Tathāgata’s majestic spiritual power and merit, I had merely joyfully cut down the grasses and trees, and cleared away all impurities until nothing remained.
Having finished sweeping the stupa, he circumambulated it eight times with a single-minded joy, joined his palms in prostration, and departed.

By virtue of this merit, after his life ended, he was reborn in the fifteenth heaven, the Ābhāsvara Heaven; there, he used various precious jewels to form a palace whose radiance shone brilliantly, standing preeminent and immeasurably sublime among all the devas.

Having exhausted his natural lifespan, he returned to become a wheel-turning sage-king one hundred times; the seven treasures appeared spontaneously, and he presided over the four quarters as their sovereign.

When that life also came to an end, he was always reborn into the families of great kings, noble clans, or elder householders, possessing immeasurable wealth and a countenance so exceptionally beautiful that it had no peer; all who saw him were filled with joy, and there were none who did not love and revere him.
When he wished to travel, the roads became naturally purified, and amidst the void, a rain of various flowers fell.

By virtue of this reverence, his place of birth was spontaneously provided; throughout ninety *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas of wandering through the cycle of existence, he was constantly born among gods and humans, enjoying natural dignity, nobility, and high status, never falling into the three miserable realms.

I recall this matter with great wonder and amazement: now that my final aspirations for merit are fully fulfilled, I have encountered the Śāstṛ, the hero among the three realms; having entered his honored Dharma, I have become a śramaṇa. My six supernormal powers are pure and penetrating, such that there is nothing I do not understand or master. All desires are forever extinguished as I have attained arhatship; free from further affliction and fever, I am cool and without heat. My mind is pure, and I have obtained great peace.
If there are those who can perform even a virtue as small as a hair toward the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha, the retribution they receive in their place of birth will be vast and inexhaustible.
"I reflect that such is the retribution for the virtuous conduct I performed in the past.
Having thus recounted his own past deeds before the Buddha, Pāṭakalī paid homage to the Buddha and withdrew to stand to one side.
In the past, when the Buddha first attained the Way, he reflected:
"Sentient beings are ignorant, possessed of inverted views, and stubbornly difficult to transform; if I were to preach the Dharma for them, who would be willing to believe and accept it?"
"It would be better for him to enter parinirvāṇa;
there is no one who comes to request the Buddha to preach the Dharma.

Knowing that the Buddha’s intention was to enter nirvāṇa, the Brahmā, together with countless hosts of Brahmās, arrived at the Buddha’s location in the time it takes a person to bend and extend their arm. We pray that the World-Honored One, with great kindness, great compassion, and immeasurable pity, will accept our invitation—indeed, graciously accept our invitation—to open and expound the treasury of the Dharma and bestow the light of wisdom.”
The Buddha told Brahmā:
"Sentient beings are difficult to awaken; they are deluded and hold inverted views. Even if I were to preach the Dharma of the sutras for them, who would be willing to believe and accept it?"
"I had better attain nirvana early.
Thereupon, Brahmā entreated him again, saying:

"The sentient beings of the three realms have long remained in darkness; it is only after hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas that a Buddha appears. Just as the udumbara flower appears only at rare intervals, so too is a Buddha difficult to encounter."
I only pray that the Tathāgata will again bestow great compassion upon me, awaken my ignorance, and preach the Dharma.

Since time immemorial, throughout countless kalpas, the World-Honored One has relinquished his body and life—his head, eyes, marrow, brain, flesh, muscles, bones, blood, kingdoms, cities, wives, and children—bestowing them all upon others. For the sake of sentient beings, he has given rise to a great and solemn vow: "I shall act as a great light for all sentient beings."
"In the distant past, incalculable kalpas ago, there was a great king of Jambudvīpa named Duṣyaṇaśrī.
He was supremely compassionate, benevolent, courageous, and handsome; he ruled over eighty-four thousand nations, and his realm was prosperous while its people lived in peace and happiness."
At that time, the king sat in his main hall and reflected to himself:

"This lady enjoys such natural splendor, honor, nobility, wealth, and pleasure; all of this arises from the practice of various virtues and the cultivation of wisdom in previous lives. It is for this reason that she now possesses these natural endowments.

Yet, having obtained these natural blessings, she is deluded by sensual desires; she does not contemplate impermanence, nor does she know how to continue cultivating merit for future lives, remaining like a beast that eats its fill all day long without applying its mind to anything."
"One who is wise should only cultivate the daily benefits of the True Dharma of wisdom.
Having reflected thus, he addressed his attendant ministers:
"Summon those among you who possess wisdom to preach the Dharma for me; I wish to hear it."
The ministers received these instructions and dispatched envoys to various kingdoms to invite those who were clever and possessed of great wisdom.
At that time, there was a brahmin whose learning was vast and whose wisdom was preeminent; he came to respond to the king’s summons.
The ministers addressed the king, saying:
"There is now a Brahmin, wise and profoundly learned, who has arrived outside the gate.

Upon hearing this, the king was filled with joy; he immediately went out to welcome him, prostrated himself at his feet in salutation, prepared a precious throne for him, and provided him with sweet delicacies. When the meal was finished, the Brahmin rinsed his mouth and washed his hands.

The king said to the brahmin, "I have long heard of your virtue, and thus I have traveled from afar to request your presence. I only pray that the Great Seer will expound the Dharma for me. He replied:
"Since I began my studies, I have labored diligently for many years; Great King, why do you wish to hear [the Dharma] so abruptly?
The king said to the brahmin, "If you require a kingdom, a city, or precious jewels, I shall provide you with whatever you desire."

He replied: "I have no need for precious jewels, kingdoms, cities, wives, children, elephants, or horses. Great King, if you can cut the flesh from your own body to make a thousand lamps, and if you can do so, I shall preach the Dharma for you; if you cannot do so, the sutras and the Dharma are difficult to hear."
The king thought to himself:

"Throughout countless kalpas, the number of times I have lost my body is beyond calculation, yet never once was it for the sake of the Dharma. Now, for the sake of the Dharma, I offer my body as a lamp; this is truly a most excellent and auspicious thing."
The king was greatly delighted and replied to the brāhmaṇa, saying:
"As you have commanded, I shall immediately carry it out; I dare not disobey your order. The brāhmaṇa said:
"It would be most excellent if you could do so!
When will it take place?
The king replied again:
"Seven days from now, I shall do so.
The King then commanded his ministers to proclaim to the Great Kings of all nations:
"Seven days from now, for the sake of hearing the Dharma, I shall set a thousand lamps upon my body."
"Those who wish to come and see the King shall all assemble at the great kingdom.
Following these instructions, the ministers simultaneously dispatched envoys to eighty-four thousand nations, saying:
"In seven days from now, the Great King shall ignite a thousand lamps upon his body."
"Let all kings, ministers, and subjects who wish to come and see the king hasten here and arrive at the great kingdom.
At that time, when the kings, ministers, and subjects heard this, they were struck with such alarm as if they had lost their parents; their wailing and weeping shook the entire Jambudvīpa.
All the kings, ministers, and subjects gathered together, and the king commanded his attendants:
"Prepare seats upon a vast, wide, and level ground.
The ministers received the command and immediately prepared couches and seats upon that expansive land.

At that time, having finished his meal, the King was seated upon his throne, preceded and followed by his consorts, twenty thousand court ladies, and ten thousand ministers. Then all the consorts, court ladies, kings, ministers, and the common people simultaneously struck their breasts before the King and, with one voice, addressed him, saying:
"We pray only that the Heavenly King will show us great kindness and compassion, and immeasurable pity!"
"For our sake, do not burn a thousand lamps upon your body.
The King replied to the various kings, ministers, subjects, ladies, and court ladies:

"Since incalculable kalpas past, I have undergone countless destructions of my body through birth and death within the five realms of existence, yet I have never sacrificed my life for the sake of the Dharma."

Now, for the sake of the Dharma, I offer my own body as a lamp; taking these merits, I employ them to seek the Buddha-way, universally acting as a great light for immeasurable sentient beings throughout the ten directions, and removing the darkness of ignorance and the three poisons from all beings.
"When I attain Buddhahood, I shall bestow upon you the light of wisdom to illuminate and eliminate birth and death, opening the gate of Nirvana so that you may enter the Dharma of peace and security.
You must not abandon my unsurpassed resolve for the Way."
At that time, all those gathered remained silent.

Then the Great King immediately took a sword and handed it to his attendants, commanding them to cut his body so as to create a place for a thousand lamps; they extracted flesh from his body as deep as large coins and poured ghee and oil into the hollows to light a thousand lamps.
Once the wick had been securely placed, he said to the brāhmaṇa,
"First preach the Dharma, and only then light the lamp.
But the brāhmaṇa, for the sake of the king, spoke only this single verse:
"‘What is constant comes to an end; that which is high shall also fall.
There is separation from those who meet, and for those who are born, there is death.

Having heard this verse, the King was filled with joy and leaped for gladness. He commanded his ministers, queens, and court ladies to all receive and recite it. He immediately inscribed the verse on the gates, streets, and alleys, and decreed that all the people must chant it. He further ordered that the kings, ministers, and subjects throughout Jambudvīpa should likewise chant it."
Then the Great King said to the brahmin,
"Now you may light the lamp.
The king then made this vow:

"Now, for the sake of the Dharma, I offer my own body as a lamp. I do not seek to become a noble wheel-turning king, nor anything up to the status of a Heavenly Emperor or the kings of the various worlds and their worldly splendors; nor do I seek the realization of the Two Vehicles. Upholding these merits, I vow to seek the unsurpassed, right, and true path, so that for all sentient beings of the five realms throughout the ten directions, I may act as a great Dharma-light to illuminate all darkness."
At that time, having made this vow, the king immediately caused the three-thousandfold world system to quake in six ways; even up to the Śuddhāvāsa Heaven, all the palaces shook throughout.
At that time, the devas and humans were filled with great alarm and fear, asking:
"What auspicious omen is this that causes the earth to tremble so violently?
They immediately used their divine eyes to observe Jambudvīpa and saw that for the sake of the Dharma, the Bodhisattva had lit a thousand lamps upon his own body, giving rise to a great vow.
"It was for this reason alone.
At that time, all the devas and humans descended and beheld the Bodhisattva’s body ablaze with a thousand lamps; countless devas wept in sorrow, raining down tears.
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, stood before the king and praised him, saying:
"Excellent! Excellent!"
"For the sake of the Dharma, you do not begrudge even your own body or life; what is it that you seek?

The Bodhisattva replied, "I do not seek to become a Wheel-Turning Sage King, a Heavenly Lord, a Mara King, or a Brahma King; nor do I seek forms, sounds, fragrances, or tastes. I do not seek the state of an Arhat or a Pratyekabuddha. I shall take these merits and use them to seek the Unsurpassed, Right, and True Way, universally bestowing the light of wisdom upon immeasurable sentient beings throughout the ten directions, illuminating and dispelling the darkness of the three poisons and ignorance within them, so that they may be freed from all suffering and attain the peace and bliss of Nirvana."
Then Śakra, Lord of the Devas, again asked the king:
"While your body was set ablaze with a thousand lamps, did you not experience pain and distress, or did you feel any regret?
The king replied to Śakra:
"I did not consider it painful, nor do I have any regret.
The Heavenly Emperor asked again:
"If you have no regret, what serves as proof?"
Thereupon, the king made this vow:
"For the sake of the Dharma, I shall today kindle a thousand lamps with my own body; by means of this merit, I seek the unsurpassed, perfect, and true path."
"If I am truly destined to attain Buddhahood, may these sores from the thousand lamps be immediately healed; may my body be restored to its original state, free from any scars.
Having spoken these words, his body was instantly restored, and he was once again free of scars, appearing more upright, beautiful, and magnificent than before.
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, countless devas, kings and ministers, ladies and court attendants, and immeasurable commoners, with one voice and in unison, all praised him, saying:
“Excellent! Excellent!”
"Excellent! they exclaimed, marveling at such an unprecedented occurrence. Filled with joy and leaping for gladness, they all vowed to practice the teachings of the ten wholesome actions.
The Buddha said:
“The king at that time was none other than myself; the brahmin was Devadatta.
Thus did the Bodhisattva seek to cultivate wisdom with such diligence.”
