The Buddha asked Sudatta,
"Should a householder practice giving or not?
Sudatta replied to the Buddha:
"One should practice giving.
Should one give much,
or should one give little?"
"Should one practice giving with a favorable intention,
or should one practice giving with an unfavorable intention?
The Buddha told Sudatta:
"Now, regarding giving: though what is given may be much, the reward obtained is small;
though the gift may be small, the reward obtained is great.
What is meant by 'giving much yet obtaining a small reward'? "
Although one may give much in alms, if it is done without a sincere heart, without a heart of reverence, without great joy, and with arrogance and self-conceit;
and if the recipient of the gift holds false and inverted views rather than right view, being no noble person (ārya)— then despite the abundance of what is given, the reward obtained will be small.
It is like sowing seeds in poor soil: though the seeds planted are many, the harvest of fruit is very small.
What is meant by giving little yet obtaining great merit?
It is when that which is given, though small, is given with joy, given with a pure mind, given with reverence, and given without expectation of reward.
If one gives to those who are superior persons— namely, Buddhas, pratyekabuddhas, śramaṇas of the four paths, and those who possess right view—
the reward obtained will be vast and great, even though the gift itself was small.
"It is just like a fertile field: though what is sown is small, the harvest of fruit is very great.
The Buddha told Sudatta:

"I recall that in a past life, there was a Wheel-Turning King in this Jambudvīpa named Potalaka. The king had a thousand sons and ruled over the four continents; in this Jambudvīpa alone, there were eighty-four thousand kingdoms."

At that time, there was a brahmin named Pilinda, whose body was golden in color and peerlessly handsome. He was intelligent and wise, possessing knowledge of the movements of heaven and earth, as well as mastery of medical prescriptions and exorcistic rites. Above, he understood celestial phenomena; below, he examined terrestrial geography; and in between, he knew the nature of human affairs. There were no classical texts to which he had not attained thorough penetration, and he was benevolent and compassionate toward all beings.
The king loved and revered him deeply; likewise, the eighty-four thousand kings and the people of the land all honored and respected him as their teacher and leader.
This great master was for this great king, not for Pāṭaliputra.
For what reason?

King Prasenajit governed the state and rectified the people by consulting the Great Master Vairāṭīputra on every matter before providing instruction; thus, none among the kings, ministers, or subjects failed to rejoice.

At that time, the Great King received the scriptures from Bimbisāra; he also proclaimed to eighty-four thousand minor kings, ministers, crown princes, and all the people, that they too should receive the scriptures from Bimbisāra and study wisdom.
The kings, ministers, and subjects all received the scriptures from Pilinda, and there was none who did not rejoice, all saying:
"This is Brahmā who has come to transform us for our own benefit."
"He is no ordinary man.
At that time, the eighty-four thousand kings received his teachings on wisdom; their minds were opened and enlightened, and they all rejoiced greatly.

Eighty-four thousand minor kings each brought one white elephant adorned with gold and silver, one swift horse likewise adorned with gold and silver, and one ox likewise adorned with gold and silver; they also brought one exquisite woman of incomparable beauty, wearing magnificent ornaments and garments made of the seven treasures. They presented golden bowls filled with silver grain, silver bowls filled with gold grain, lapis lazuli bowls filled with gold grain, and crystal bowls filled with gold grain. They also provided chariots made of gold and decorated with the seven treasures; there were eighty-four thousand such sets for each king, all of which they offered as tribute to the Great Master of Bārāṇasī.
"At that time, King Prasenajit, hearing that the minor kings had presented offerings to Bimbisāra, was greatly delighted and thought:
'I too shall present wealth and treasures to the Great Teacher Bimbisāra.'"

Immediately, he adorned eighty-four thousand celestial maidens, their bodies graced with exquisite necklaces and ornaments of the seven treasures and pearls; eighty-four thousand white elephants were draped with pure gold trappings; eighty-four thousand horses were likewise draped with gold and silver trappings; eighty-four thousand oxen were entirely decorated with gold; eighty-four thousand golden bowls were filled with silver grain; eighty-four thousand silver bowls were filled with golden grain; eighty-four thousand lapis lazuli bowls were filled with golden grain; eighty-four thousand crystal bowls were all filled with golden grain; and eighty-four thousand chariots were entirely decorated with gold trappings—all of which he offered to Vaiśālī.
Having received [the inheritance], Virūḍhaka reflected that all these possessions—wealth, treasures, elephants, horses, and chariots—are impermanent and lack solidity. He said to the Great King:
"All property and possessions are impermanent and subject to destruction; I have no need for them, as I intend to practice charity to relieve the poor and destitute."
Upon hearing these words, the king was greatly delighted and commanded his ministers to beat the drums and proclaim a royal edict:
"Let all the poor, the orphaned, the elderly, the brahmins, and the śramaṇas within Jambudvīpa assemble; at Bimbisāra, a great dāna will be established."
When the people heard the proclamation, they gathered like clouds rising; the strong and the weak supported one another as they all arrived.
At that time, Bilara wished to wash the hands of the brahmin, but though he tilted his *kamaṇḍalu*, no water came forth, and he was filled with great sorrow.
"Now, what fault could there be in my great sacrifice?
Is my intention not pure?
Or is that which I have bestowed not excellent?"
"For what reason does the water not come forth? At that moment, a celestial being spoke from the midst of the air to Piliyan:

"Your current act of giving is most excellent and peerless; your mind is pure and stainless, such that none can surpass it. Your merit is foremost in the world, with none above it. However, those to whom you have given are all followers of heterodox and false views; they are not the class of pure and noble gentlemen who are worthy of receiving your offerings and respect. For this reason, the water does not come forth."
Thereupon, having heard the words of the deva, Bīraṇa’s mind was immediately opened and resolved, and he made this vow:
"If my application of this offering shall now bring about the attainment of the unsurpassed, right, and true path, exactly as I have prayed, then let this water I pour down fall into my own hand."
Having finished making this vow, he then tilted his water jar, and the water immediately came forth and fell into the palm of his hand.
The devas in the sky praised him from above, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!"
"As you have wished, you shall attain Buddhahood before long.
At that time, Pūraṇa bestowed upon the poor and destitute all necessities, such as clothing, bedding, food, and drink.
"For twelve years, I gave away my elephants, horses, precious treasures, and beautiful women in alms, without hoarding anything.
The Buddha told Sudatta:
"The Brahmin Bhīṣma at that time was none other than myself."
At that time, my gifts were excellent and my mind was excellent, yet the recipients were not; thus, although what I gave was much, the reward obtained was very small.
Now, my Dharma is truly wonderful and pure, and my disciples are genuine; therefore, although what is given may be little, the reward obtained is very great.

Thus, the merit of all the almsgiving performed by Bimbisāra during twelve years, as well as the almsgiving practiced by all the people of Jambudvīpa, when calculated, does not equal that of giving to a single *srotāpanna*; its blessing is far greater and surpasses them all.

The merit obtained from providing for a hundred *srotāpannas*, together with the previous gift to the people of Jambudvīpa by Piliyakkha, does not equal that of giving to a single *sakṛdāgāmin*; the latter’s merit is far greater and surpasses the former.

Even if one were to give alms to a hundred Sakṛdāgāmins, a hundred Srotāpannas, and furthermore bestow gifts upon all the people of Jambudvīpa as previously described, the merit and reward obtained would not equal that of giving to a single Anāgāmin; the latter's merit is many times greater and surpasses the former.

The merit and reward obtained from giving to one hundred anāgāmins, one hundred sakṛdāgāmins, and one hundred srotāpannas—along with the aforementioned people of Jambudvīpa—is not equal to that of giving to a single arhat; the latter's merit is far greater and surpasses the former.

Even if one were to give alms to a hundred arhats, a hundred anāgāmins, a hundred sakṛdāgāmins, and a hundred srotāpannas, as well as to all the people of Jambudvīpa from Pāṭaliputra mentioned previously, the merit of such giving would not equal that of giving to a single pratyekabuddha; the latter’s blessing is far greater and surpasses the former.

Even if one were to give alms to a hundred pratyekabuddhas, a hundred arhats, a hundred anāgāmins, a hundred sakṛdāgāmins, and a hundred srotāpannas, as well as giving to all the people of Jambudvīpa as previously described, the merit obtained would not equal that of building stūpas, monasteries, and vihāras, and providing offerings of clothing, bedding, seats, and food to the Saṃgha of monks and śramaṇas from the four quarters—past, future, and present—who provide for their necessary requirements; when calculated, this merit surpasses all the merit produced by the former acts.

Even if one were to erect stupas, monasteries, and vihāras, and bestow gifts upon pratyekabuddhas, arhats, anāgāmins, sakṛdāgāmins, and srotāpannas—along with all the people of Jambudvīpa from the past up to the present—the merit and virtue of such giving would not equal that of giving to a single Buddha; the latter’s merit is so vast that it can no longer be calculated.

Even if one were to make offerings to the Buddha by erecting stupas, monasteries, and vihāras, or to pratyekabuddhas, arhats, anāgāmins, sakṛdāgāmins, and srotāpannas—along with all the people of Jambudvīpa who have previously performed acts of giving—the merit obtained from such offerings does not equal that of a person who, within a single day, takes the three refuges and the eightfold fast, or observes the five precepts. The merit thus acquired far exceeds the previously mentioned blessings, surpassing them by a factor of hundreds, thousands, tens of thousands, and millions beyond comparison.

Furthermore, the merit of observing the precepts, combined with all the merits previously accumulated from making offerings to Buddhas, Pratyekabuddhas, and those on the four paths, as well as the merit from the offerings made by the people of Jambudvīpa at Piṇḍavana—all this does not equal the merit obtained by practicing seated meditation and contemplating sentient beings with loving-kindness for even the duration of a single meal; it exceeds the former by hundreds of thousands of millions of times.

It surpasses all the merit previously accumulated by the people of Jambudvīpa—such as the acts of giving, including offerings made to those of the four paths and to *pratyekabuddhas*, the construction of stūpas and monasteries, and even offerings up to those made to the Buddha—as well as the merit of observing the precepts, practicing meditation, and maintaining thoughts of loving-kindness toward sentient beings. When these virtues are combined, they do not equal hearing the Dharma and holding it in one’s heart, contemplating the Four Truths and the dharmas of impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self, and the tranquil extinction of *nirvāṇa*. Compared to all the merits performed previously, this is the most honored, the foremost, and unsurpassed.
Thereupon, upon hearing the Dharma, Sudatta was filled with immeasurable joy; his body and mind were purified, and he attained the stage of Anāgāmin.

He possessed only five gold coins; each day he would take one coin to offer to the Buddha, one coin to offer to the Dharma, one coin to offer to the Saṃgha, one coin for his own sustenance, and one coin as capital.
He continued in this manner every day, yet there was always one coin remaining, which never came to an end.
He immediately received the five precepts and, kneeling with his right knee on the ground, addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Today my lustful mind has been severed; dwelling as a householder, what should I do?
The Buddha told Sudatta:
"Just as your mind is now pure and free from further desire, you should return home and ask your wives:
'Now my lustful mind has been extinguished; each of you may follow what you please.'"
"Those who require a husband may follow their own inclinations; if you wish to remain here, I shall provide you with food and clothing.
Sudatta accepted these instructions, paid homage to the Buddha, and returned home to ask his wives:

"I have now forever exhausted all craving and desire, and no longer have any lustful affairs. If any of you require a husband, each may follow her own preference; those who wish to remain here, I shall provide them with food and clothing so that they lack for nothing."
The women each followed their own inclinations according to their pleasure.

At that time, there was a woman who had ground grain into flour. A young goat came and pulled at the barley; having no other recourse, she seized a fire-brand to strike the goat. Fire from the tip of the brand caught on the goat's wool; the goat, seeking relief from the heat, rubbed itself against the elephant stable. The elephant stable caught fire and burned the king’s elephant. The elephant’s body was scorched and mangled, so the woman killed a monkey and used its carcass to beat the elephant’s body.
A deva spoke these verses from mid-air:
"At the edge of anger and strife, one should not remain;
Like horned cattle butting each other, The fly and the moth perish therein."
"A maidservant fought with a goat, and a monkey died while sitting [nearby].
The wise keep far from such suspicions; do not dwell with fools.
King Prasenajit commanded his ministers to establish a boundary:
"From this day forward, it is forbidden to light fires, lamps, or candles at night; anyone who violates this shall be fined one thousand taels of gold.

At that time, Sudatta, having attained the Way while remaining a householder, practiced seated meditation day and night. During the first watch of the night, he would light a lamp and sit in meditation; he would rest at midnight, and at cockcrow, he would again light a lamp and sit in meditation.
The spies captured him and, holding a lamp, presented him to the King,
saying, "He must pay a fine.
Sudatta then addressed the King:
"I am now so poor that I possess not even a hundred coins; with what, then, shall I pay the king's fine?
The king, in a rage, commanded his officers:
"Take Sudatta immediately to prison and place him under guard!"
When the Four Heavenly Kings saw that Sudatta was imprisoned in the jail, during the first watch of the night they descended and said to Sudatta:
"We shall give you money to pay the king's fine so that you may come out."
Sudatta replied, "The King shall naturally find joy and his mind will be liberated; there is no need for money.
Having finished preaching the sutra for the Four Heavenly Kings, the kings departed.
At midnight, Śakra, the Lord of Devas, again descended to visit him; after Sudatta had finished preaching the Dharma for him, Śakra departed.
Next, during the latter part of the night, Brahmā descended again to see Sudatta and preached the Dharma for him; then Brahmā also departed.
At that time, while the king was on his terrace at night, he saw a light from fire atop the prison. The next day, the king immediately dispatched a messenger to tell Sudatta:
"Sitting in confinement for the sake of fire, you have no sense of shame; you continue to kindle fires once again."
Sudatta replied, "I have not lit a fire;
if a fire had been lit, there would be signs such as smoke and ash.
He spoke again to Sudatta:

"In the first watch of the night there are four fires; in the middle watch of the night there is one fire twice as large as the previous ones; and in the last watch of the night there is yet another fire that is twice as large as the preceding one.
What is this 'fire that does not burn'?"
Sudatta replied, "This is not fire.

During the first watch of the night, the Four Heavenly Kings descended to see me; during the middle watch, the second heaven, Śakra Devendra, descended to see me; and during the last watch, the seventh heaven, Brahmā, descended to see me. These are the radiant flames from the bodies of these devas, not fire."
Upon hearing these words, the messenger went at once to inform the king; when the king heard this, his heart was struck with alarm and his hair stood on end.
The king said, "This man’s merit and virtue are so extraordinary; how could I now insult or humiliate him?"
He immediately commanded his officials, saying, "Release him quickly; do not cause any delay.
They then released him and let him go.
Sudatta emerged and went to where the Buddha was; he prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, withdrew to sit, and listened to the Dharma.

King Prasenajit immediately prepared his carriage and followed him to the Buddha’s location. When the people saw the king, they all vacated their seats and rose, but Sudatta alone remained focused on the flavor of the Dharma and did not rise upon seeing the king.
The king felt a slight resentment, thinking:
"This is my subject; harboring a spirit of contempt, he does not rise when he sees me.
Thus, he conceived a heart of indignation.
The Buddha, knowing his intention, desisted and did not preach the Dharma.
The king addressed the Buddha, saying,
"I pray that you will preach the sutras and the Dharma."
The Buddha said to the king:
"Now is not the time for me to preach the Dharma to you, O King.
Why is it not the right time? [Because]..."

People give rise to anger and resentment, harboring knots of enmity that they do not untie; they may give rise to lustful desire, becoming intoxicated and infatuated with female beauty, or be arrogant and conceited, lacking a heart of reverence.
Their minds are defiled and turbid, such that even when they hear the sublime Dharma, they cannot understand it. For these reasons, now is not the time for me to preach the Dharma to you, O King.
Upon hearing the Buddha’s words, the king thought to himself:
"Because of this man, I have today suffered two setbacks; furthermore, I have given rise to anger and been unable to hear the Dharma."
Having paid homage to the Buddha, he departed. Once outside, he commanded his attendants:
"If this man comes out, cut off his head immediately.
Having spoken these words, at that very moment, tigers, wolves, lions, and other venomous beasts came from all four directions and surrounded the king.
When the king saw this, he was seized with great terror and returned to where the Buddha was.
The Buddha asked the Great King,
"Why have you returned?"
The king said to the Buddha,
“I saw him returning in such a state of terror.
The Buddha told the king:
"Do you know this man? The king replied, "I do not."
The Buddha said:
"This man has attained the stage of Anāgāmin; it was because he sat and rose with an evil intention toward this person that such a thing occurred.
If he were not a Non-returner, Your Majesty would surely be in peril and unable to be saved."
Upon hearing the Buddha’s words, the king was immediately seized with great terror; he then prostrated himself before Sudatta in repentance and spread out four sheepskins before him.
The king said, “These are my subjects, yet to have humiliated them was truly most difficult.”
Sudatta spoke again: "I am poor, and thus it is also extremely difficult for me to practice giving.
Śīlavant was serving as a judge of justice for the kingdom when he was captured by bandits.
The bandit said to him,
"If you say you have not seen me, I shall release you;
otherwise, I will kill you."
Śīlavant thought to himself,
"If I now speak a falsehood and commit an unrighteous act, and should fall into hell, who will deliver me?
Having reflected thus, he spoke to the bandits:
"I would rather have my head cut off than ever speak a falsehood.
The bandit then released him.
When peril was imminent, to refrain from lying and to carefully practice the True Dharma is indeed exceedingly difficult.
Furthermore, there was a deva named Śakali who declared of himself:
"I observed the eightfold fast and lay upon a high tower.
A celestial jade maiden came to me; that I did not accept her, despite having maintained my prohibitive precepts, is truly most difficult."
Thereupon, each of the four men spoke thus for himself, and immediately before the Buddha they uttered these verses:
“For the poor, giving is difficult; for the wealthy and noble, patience is difficult;
in perilous circumstances, upholding the precepts is difficult; in youth, renouncing desire is difficult.”

After the Buddha had spoken these verses, he further expounded the Dharma. The king, his ministers, and the common people were all greatly delighted; they paid homage to the Buddha and departed. Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was staying at the Kalandakanivāpa Monastery in Veṇuvana near Rājagṛha. In the village of Uruvilvā there was a spring containing a venomous dragon named Caṇḍāli, who was extremely fierce and malevolent. He would release hail and frost, destroying the five grains so that they did not ripen, causing the people to suffer from hunger.
At that time, there was a brahmin who, through incantations, subdued the dragons so that they would not produce hail or frost, and the five grains ripened in abundance.
After many years had passed, this brahmin eventually grew old and infirm, and his magical arts no longer worked.

At that time, there was a robust brahmin who was fluent in incantations; raising his voice, he recited mantras, whereupon the clouds dispersed and prevented hail and frost from falling, so that the five grains ripened in abundance.
The people were delighted and said to the brahmin, "Please stay here;
we shall provide for you together so that you lack for nothing.
The brahmin replied:
"Very well," he replied, and so he stayed.
There he constantly gathered and collected [wealth], ensuring that the Śūdra Brahmin never lacked for anything.
Since the Buddha arrived in the kingdom and extensively preached the Dharma, people of all ages have received his transformative teachings, and many have attained the Way.

All the dragons and spirits have become virtuous and no longer commit evil or cause harm; winds and rains come at their proper seasons, the five grains are abundant and cheap, and they no longer provide for the needs of the Brahmins.
The brāhmaṇa went to them and asked for it, but the people instead spat upon him, reviled him, and would not give it to him.
At that time, anger arose in the brāhmaṇa’s heart:
"Having been satiated by the power of my grace, they have instead treated me with contempt."
Desiring to destroy the people and the kingdom, he asked a person:
"How can one obtain what the heart desires?
The person replied to him:
"If one offers food to the four honored disciples of the Buddha, one will surely attain their wishes according to what they desire.

At that time, the brahmin immediately prepared a meal and invited Mahākāśyapa, Śāriputra, Maudgalyāyana, and Aniruddha. When these four honored ones arrived, he paid them homage with a sincere heart and requested his wish:
"I now take this merit from my offering and pray that I may become a powerful venomous dragon to destroy this country; I must surely attain this wish."
At that time, Śāriputra, observing with his divine eye, considered what kind of vow he sought;
he knew that the brahmin was thinking in his heart of a vow to become a venomous dragon in order to destroy this country.
At that time, Śāriputra said to the brahmin:
"Do not make such a vow; why would you seek to take on the harmful and evil body of a dragon or a snake?
If you wish to become a Wheel-Turning Sage King, or Śakra Devendra, or Māra, or Brahmā, all of these can be attained."
"Why would one use this evil body for an undesirable vow?
At that time, the brahmin replied to Śāriputra, "I have sought this vow for a long time and am now about to obtain it; I do not desire any other vow."
Then, the brahmin raised his five fingers and water immediately flowed forth.
Seeing that his resolve was firm and that such a sign had been manifested, Śāriputra remained silent and ceased [his questioning].

At that time, the Brahmin, his wife, and their two sons all made a vow to become dragons; upon death, they received dragon bodies, possessing great supernatural power yet being exceedingly venomous and evil. They then killed the Dragon Sāṇḍili, seized his abode, and began to unleash winds and rains, causing hail and frost to fall in great abundance. This destroyed the five grains, leaving only straw and chaff behind; consequently, the dragon was named Aparajita.

The wife was named Bishouni. The dragon had two sons, the first of whom was named Jishanini. The people were suffering from such widespread famine that many died; furthermore, due to an epidemic, countless others perished.
At that time, King Ajātaśatru went to where the Buddha was, prostrated himself with his head at the Buddha’s feet, knelt for a long time, and addressed the Buddha:

“The people within my realm have been harmed by evil dragons and pestilential demons; those who have died are beyond counting. I only pray that the World-Honored One, out of great kindness and great compassion, will take pity on all beings and grant protection to ward off this disaster.”
The Buddha granted his consent.

Then, on the following morning, the World-Honored One donned his robes, took up his bowl, and entered the city to beg for food. Having gone to the Dragon Spring and finished his meal, he washed his bowl; the water used for washing flowed back into the spring.

The dragon, filled with great wrath, immediately emerged from the water, exhaling poisonous gas and spitting fire toward the Buddha; the Buddha caused water to issue from his own body to extinguish it.
Again, he rained down large hailstones, which were transformed in mid-air into celestial flowers.
Again, he rained down large stones, which were transformed into exquisite ornaments.
Again, he rained down swords and blades, which were transformed into the seven precious jewels;
he manifested as a rākṣasa, but the Buddha further manifested as King Vaiśravaṇa, and the rākṣasa was immediately extinguished.
The dragon again transformed into a great elephant with its trunk grasping a sharp sword, but the Buddha instantly transformed into a great lion king, and the elephant then vanished.
Just as he had manifested himself as a dragon, the Buddha further transformed himself into a king of the garuḍas, and the dragon fled in haste.

Exhausting all his supernatural powers, the dragon was unable to harm the Buddha; he plunged into a spring. Then the Vajrapāṇi Māhapuruṣa raised his vajra-pestle and struck a mountain, causing it to collapse so that half fell into the spring.
Desiring to flee and go out, the Buddha transformed the spring water so that it entirely became a great mass of fire.
As he urgently sought to break through and escape, the World-Honored One then stepped upon the dragon’s head, and the dragon was unable to depart.
The dragon was then subdued; kneeling for a long time, he addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
Today I have particularly witnessed bitter cruelty."
The Buddha said to the nāga,
"Why do you harbor malice and afflict sentient beings?
The nāga then prostrated with his head at the Buddha's feet, knelt for a long time, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I pray that you release me; I shall respectfully accept whatever the World-Honored One commands.
The Buddha told the dragon, "You shall receive the five precepts and become an upāsaka."

The dragon, along with his wife and children, all received the five precepts and became upāsakas. With hearts of loving-kindness, they practiced virtue, and frost and hail no longer occurred. Wind and rain fell in their proper seasons, the five grains ripened in abundance, and all the pestilential spirits fled away toward Vaiśālī.
The people of Magadha were satiated, their various ailments were cured, and they subsequently attained peace and happiness.

In Vaiśālī, however, those who died from pestilence were exceedingly numerous. Hearing that the Buddha was in Magadha, having subdued the evil dragon and caused the pestilence to vanish, the King of Vaiśālī immediately dispatched a messenger to the place where the Buddha was.
Thereupon, the messenger proceeded to where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, knelt for a long time, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“The King has specifically sent me here to prostrate and inquire after the health of the Tathāgata, the Great Sage!”
The number of those who have died from the plague in our country is vast;
we only pray that the World-Honored One, out of great compassion and pity, will extend Your grace to cover our land, so that by the humble presence of Your majestic light, all may be fully delivered.
The kingdom of Vaiśālī and the kingdom of Magadha had long harbored mutual resentment; when King Ajātaśatru heard that a pestilence was spreading through Vaiśālī, he rejoiced greatly.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the messenger from Vaiśālī:
"I have already accepted King Ajātaśatru’s invitation for ninety days, and it has not yet concluded; you should go yourself and speak to King Ajātaśatru."
The messenger addressed the Buddha, saying:
“The two kingdoms have long harbored mutual resentment; if I go there now, I will surely be put to death.
The Buddha said to the messenger:
"You shall merely act as a messenger for the Buddha; no one will ever be able to kill you.
The Buddha spoke again to the messenger, saying:
"Tell King Ajātaśatru:..."
"Because he has turned toward the Tathāgata with repentance for the grave crime of patricide, he shall undergo only five hundred days of worldly punishment within hell and shall then be liberated."

The messenger immediately accepted the command and went to the king’s gate. When the king and his ministers heard that the messenger from Vaiśālī was outside the gate, they were all filled with indignation and deliberated together, saying:
“We shall cut off his head, gouge out his ears and nose, and crush his bones until they are like flour.”
The messenger entered before the palace and proclaimed loudly,
"The World-Honored One has sent me to the presence of the Great King.
Hearing that he was a messenger from the Buddha, everyone was filled with joy.
The king asked the messenger, "The Buddha has sent you here; what are his instructions?
The messenger then replied:
“The Buddha replies to the Great King:

‘Because you have used this evil and rebellious crime of killing your father to repent before the Tathāgata, you shall suffer the retribution for five hundred days of the world while remaining in hell, after which you shall immediately be able to depart.’”
"You should only reproach yourself, reform your past, and cultivate the future; do not harbor grief or anxiety.
Upon hearing these words, the king was filled with such joy and exultation that he could not contain himself:
"I have committed a heinous crime, yet there is still a time for my release from hell."
He then bowed his head in prostration toward the Buddha from afar.
The king said to the messenger,
"That you have been able to bring me this news is beyond words for its joy."
"Whatever wish you seek, I shall grant it to you as you desire!
The messenger addressed the King, saying:

"An epidemic is raging in the kingdom of Vaiśālī; we wish to invite the Buddha to grace our realm with his presence, hoping for complete salvation. We only pray that Your Majesty will permit the Buddha’s messenger to depart."
The King approved of this and replied to the messenger, saying: "Tell your Great King:

'From the city gate to the banks of the Ganges, I shall have the road prepared and strewn with flowers; I shall set up banners and streamers reaching to the banks of the Ganges, and the entire military force of my kingdom shall escort the World-Honored One to the banks of the Ganges.

You, likewise, should have the road leveled from the city of Vaiśālī to the banks of the Ganges, scattering flowers and incense and setting up banners and streamers reaching to the banks of the Ganges; let all the ministers, soldiers, and citizens of Vaiśālī come together to welcome the Buddha to the banks of the Ganges.'"
"If you can do so, I permit you to go as the Buddha's messenger; if you cannot, I shall not release you to go.

Having heard the king’s command, the messenger from Vaiśālī was filled with joy and leaped for gladness; he immediately took his leave and returned to the Buddha’s presence, prostrated himself with his head at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed him in this manner.
The Buddha granted his consent.
He then took leave of the Buddha, prostrated himself, and departed; returning to Vaiśālī, he reported these words to the king.
Upon hearing what was said, the king was greatly delighted.
"We too must plant roots of merit within our own country," they said, and immediately issued a decree to level and repair the roads.

From the city gates to the banks of the Ganges, they ensured everything was completely purified; they scattered various flowers, burned many kinds of famous incense, and erected numerous banners and streamers. King Vaiśālī, together with all the ministers and citizens of the kingdom, struck bells and drums and performed various musical offerings as they went to the banks of the Ganges to welcome the Buddha, the World-Honored One, presenting five hundred precious parasols as an offering to him.
The King of Magadha likewise issued a proclamation:
"Repair and clear all the roads, scattering flowers and incense and erecting various banners and streamers as far as the banks of the Ganges."

Together with his ministers, subjects, and the entire military host of the kingdom, he struck bells and drums and performed various musical entertainments that shook heaven and earth. He escorted the World-Honored One to the banks of the Ganges River and presented five hundred precious parasols to the World-Honored One.

The Four Heavenly Kings, the King of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, and all others up to the King of the Nirmāṇarati Heaven each came with countless devas, bringing various rare and exquisite treasures from the heavens, diverse kinds of flowers and incense, and manifold musical instruments, as well as five hundred precious parasols, to present as offerings to the World-Honored One.

From the seventh Brahmā King up to the Śuddhāvāsa Heaven, these various heavenly kings, each accompanied by countless sons of gods, brought various exquisite celestial incense, flowers, and diverse musical instruments, and offered five hundred precious parasols to the World-Honored One.

The Asura King Vemacitra, together with countless asura subjects, brought various precious flowers, perfumes, and diverse musical instruments, along with five hundred precious parasols, and came to present them to the Buddha.

The Naga King Sagara, together with his countless retinue of nagas, each carrying various kinds of incense and performing manifold musical performances, came with five hundred precious canopies to offer them to the World-Honored One.
Of the three thousand parasols combined, he retained only one, while the remaining ones were accepted by others.
The single parasol he retained was used to provide protection for his future disciples, enabling them to receive offerings.
At that time, immeasurable numbers of devas, humans, nāgas, and asuras came to where the Buddha was. The King of Vaiśālī, along with his ministers and subjects, all said:
"The Buddha is now about to cross the Ganges; we shall together construct five hundred boats to enable the Buddha to cross the river."
The King of Magadha, along with his ministers and subjects, also said:
"Today the Buddha shall cross the water; we too shall prepare five hundred boats to enable the Buddha to cross."
The various devas each constructed five hundred precious boats, and the asuras likewise collectively constructed five hundred precious boats.
At that time, the nāgas themselves joined their bodies together to form five hundred bridges, desiring that the World-Honored One tread upon them to cross over.

At that time, the World-Honored One, seeing that the various devas, all the people, nāgas, and asuras were each filled with joy and a heart of reverence, and wishing to cause all sentient beings to universally obtain his blessing, immediately manifested transformation bodies throughout all the boats;
thus, the devas, people, nāgas, and asuras each saw the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, alone upon their own boat and not on any other boat.

When the Tathāgata had finished crossing the water, countless devas filled the void, scattering various famous flowers, burning rare and wondrous incense, and performing all kinds of music. Humans, as well as nāgas and asuras, did likewise, scattering various famous flowers, burning various blended incenses, and performing all kinds of music, delighting the World-Honored One with immeasurable joy.

At that time, the Tathāgata surveyed the devas and humans of the three realms, who were filled with joy and offered immeasurable, exultant worship to the Tathāgata. When the World-Honored One was about to speak of the Bodhisattva path he had originally practiced in his previous lives, he immediately smiled. Five-colored light issued from his mouth; this light was divided into five parts, and from the tip of each part emerged countless rays of brilliance. From the tip of each ray there arose a precious lotus flower, and upon each flower there was a manifested Buddha. One portion of the radiance shone upward, illuminating the desire realm, the form realm, and the formless realm.

The devas of the three realms, beholding that radiance and seeing the manifested buddhas, were all filled with joy; each abandoning their sensual pleasures, they came to the place where the manifested buddha was to hear him preach the Dharma.

Immeasurable devas, having heard the preaching of the Dharma, rejoiced and leaped for joy; each attained the fruit of the path—whether the stage of entering the stream, once-returning, non-returning, or arhatship—and there were those who resolved upon the Great Vehicle and entered the stage of non-retrogression.

A portion of this radiance universally illumines those in the human realm throughout the trichiliocosm; transformation Buddhas fill the world, and all people, seeing this light and beholding these transformation Buddhas, have their intense anger and resentment extinguished as they all give rise to a heart of loving-kindness. Those with raging lust find their desire eliminated as they contemplate the impurities of the body; the ignorant and blind are all awakened and realize the four marks of impermanence. Those imprisoned and confined are all released; the blind regain their sight, the deaf regain their hearing, the mute are able to speak, and those who are hunched or crippled regain the use of their limbs. All ailments and infirmities are completely healed.
All the people were filled with joy; each leaving behind their own pleasures, they came to where the Buddha was.

At that time, the various manifested Buddhas each preached the Dharma, and their minds were opened and liberated. Some attained the fruits of the stage of stream-entry, once-returning, non-returning, or arhatship; others gave rise to the aspiration for supreme, true, and correct enlightenment. Those who firmly abided in the Mahāyāna and became non-retrogressive were beyond calculation.

A portion of the light shines upon the realms of all hungry ghosts; emanated Buddhas appear throughout every part of these realms of hungry ghosts. When the hungry ghosts behold the Buddha’s light, they spontaneously become satiated and free from hunger and thirst; their bodies and minds become pure, and they are rid of all afflictions and fevers.
Upon hearing his preaching of the Dharma, all were filled with joy and the defilement of stinginess was extinguished; after their lives ended, they were all reborn in the heavens.

A portion of the light illuminated the realm of animals throughout the great trichiliocosm; when all the birds and beasts beheld the Buddha’s radiance, they were all filled with joy, and virtuous minds arose within them spontaneously.

The hearts of tigers, wolves, lions, dragons, snakes, and other venomous evils were all completely extinguished; they turned toward one another with minds of loving-kindness and did not harm each other, and after their lives ended, they were all reborn in the heavens.

A portion of this radiance shone throughout the great trichiliocosm, illuminating all places of darkness between the Iron Ring Mountains until they were completely clear and transparent. All classes of sentient beings in the various hells, upon seeing this light and beholding the manifested Buddhas, leaped for joy; the fires were extinguished, the boiling water grew cold, and the cruel tortures of punishment all came to rest, while within the freezing hells, a natural warmth spontaneously spread.

Once the sentient beings in the hells had obtained rest, they leaped for joy; each of the manifested Buddhas preached the Dharma to them, whereby their minds were opened and their intentions liberated, and they immediately reached the end of their lives and were all reborn in the heavens.
At that time, light and transformation-buddhas filled the trichiliocosm, and sentient beings in the five realms of existence all attained liberation.
Generally, for every point where the Tathāgata’s light entered, there was a corresponding response:
if he wished to speak of matters concerning the hells, the light entered through the soles of his feet.
If he intends to speak of the matters of animals, the light enters through the top of his feet;
if he intends to speak of the matters of hungry ghosts, the light enters through his ankles;
if he intends to speak of the matters of the human realm, the light enters through his thighs.
If he intends to speak of the matters of a Wheel-Turning Sage King, the light enters through the navel;
if he intends to speak of the matters of an Arhat, the light enters through the mouth;
if he intends to speak of the matters of a Pratyekabuddha, the light enters through the space between the eyebrows.
If he wished to speak of the matters of bodhisattvas, the light entered through the crown of his head;
if he wished to speak of past matters, the light entered from behind;
if he wished to speak of future or present matters, the light entered from the front.

At that time, the World-Honored One manifested a great transformation; his radiance shone universally throughout the worlds of the ten directions, and within the realm of the great trichiliocosm, a rain of various celestial flowers fell. Immeasurable musical instruments resounded spontaneously without being struck. Among the devas, humans, and the entire great assembly, there was none who did not rejoice with redoubled exultation.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One withdrew his supernormal power, and the radiance returned to circle the Buddha three times before entering through his back.
Immeasurable devas and the entire great assembly praised him with one voice:
“The merit of the Tathāgata is so lofty and immeasurable; how inconceivable it truly is!”
Thereupon Ānanda knelt with his hands joined in reverence and stepped forward to address the Buddha, saying:
"The Buddha does not smile without cause; a smile must surely have its reason.
Today the World-Honored One has smiled so joyfully; it must be that he intends to speak of his own past deeds in former lives."
The Buddha addressed Ānanda and the great assembly:

"In the distant past, immeasurable and incalculable eons ago, there was a wheel-turning monarch in this Jambudvīpa named Śuddhodana. He ruled over the four quarters of the world; in this Jambudvīpa, there were eighty-four thousand minor kings and eighty-four thousand cities."
The King possessed seven treasures:

first, the Golden Wheel Treasure. The wheel had a thousand spokes; it was forty li in length and breadth, and one hundred and twenty li in circumference. When the King desired to travel, the wheel would precede him as a guide. For those who did not submit, the golden wheel would naturally revolve above their heads, subduing them spontaneously without the need for weapons or military force.
Second is the mani-jewel treasure: placed at the top of the banner, it constantly illuminates sixteen hundred li day and night.

Third is the white elephant treasure: the body of this elephant is long, well-proportioned, and as beautiful as snow-white light; when the king mounts it, he flies naturally through the air, circling the four continents in the time it takes to eat a single meal.
Fourth is the treasure of the dark-blue horse, with vermilion-colored mane and tail; when the king mounts it, he can traverse the four continents in the time it takes to eat a single meal.
Fifth is the minister of military affairs; whenever the king desires a hundred thousand, a million, or ten million troops, they arrive spontaneously.

The six treasury ministers, whenever the king desired gold, silver, the seven treasures, clothing, bedding, food, or drink, would open both their hands; all the wealth of the seven treasures and whatever else was required would emerge from their hands according to his every wish, without ever being exhausted.

The seventh is the Jewel of the Woman (strī-ratna). She is of incomparable beauty, like a celestial maiden, and free from the impurities and blemishes of women. Her body is fragrant and pure like an *utpala* flower; when the king desires coolness, her body naturally becomes cool, and when he desires warmth, her body naturally becomes warm. Her voice is like the Brahma-voice, constantly causing the king to rejoice and leap for joy; she is thus named the Jewel of the Woman.
The king had a thousand sons, peerless in their valor.

When the king wished to go forth, a great parasol made of the seven treasures was always held above his head; he was followed by attendants with the seven treasures, and a countless multitude of ministers led and followed him from front and rear. A hundred thousand musicians played with harmonious and elegant sounds, majestic and magnificent beyond measure.
Among the king’s thousand sons, the youngest, seeing the king in such a state, asked his mother,
"Who is this king who is so majestic? His mother replied:
"This is Śuddhodana, the Great Universal Monarch who rules over the four continents; he is your father.
Do you not recognize him? The prince replied:
"When shall I become king? His mother replied again, "The king has a thousand sons;
you are the youngest of all, so you should not become king."
The Prince spoke again:
"If it is not fitting for me to become a king, what is the use of remaining at home as a layman?
He then knelt down on his right knee and addressed his mother, saying:
"I wish to be permitted to leave the household life and become a śramaṇa, going to the mountains and marshes to study the path of the sages.
His mother immediately granted her consent and said to him:
"If you attain any wisdom through your contemplation, you must certainly return and tell me."

The son immediately consented. He then shaved his head, donned the *kāṣāya*, and went to the mountain marshes to practice meditation with diligence, contemplating wisdom. Internally, he understood the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*); externally, he realized that all things are impermanent. All who receive a body are vessels for manifold suffering; even the sovereignty of a Universal Monarch (*cakravartin*), the glory of a celestial emperor, or the honor of a world-ruler within the three realms is like a magical illusion—empty and devoid of self. Things exist when conditions meet and cease when conditions part. All proceed from delusion and craving as causes for the various formations (*saṃskāra*); because of these formations, one receives every kind of body, and through the divisions of the five destinies, there arise manifold sufferings.

If there is no delusion or craving, then there are no volitional formations; because there are no volitional formations, there are no five destinies; because there are no five destinies, one does not receive a body; and because there is no body, all suffering is extinguished.

Reflecting thus, his mind was suddenly enlightened and he became a pratyekabuddha. He flew and transformed at will, his six supernatural powers (ṣaḍabhijñā) being pure and transparent without any obstruction.

In accordance with his original vow, he returned to see his mother; manifesting his supernormal powers, he ascended into the void, walking, sitting, and lying down in mid-air. Water flowed from the upper part of his body while fire issued from the lower part; fire issued from the upper part while water flowed from the lower part. He divided his single body into a hundred, a thousand, ten thousand, and countless forms, then merged them back into one.
Upon seeing him, his mother was filled with joy and leaped for gladness; she bowed her head to the ground in salutation and asked again,
"From where did you obtain food and drink?"
He replied, "I sustain myself by begging.
His mother spoke again, saying:
"Do not seek alms elsewhere; please accept my invitation.
From this day forward, may you reside within this garden; I pray that you will receive my food and drink every day, and that I too may thereby obtain merit."
At that time, the Pratyekabuddha accepted his mother’s invitation and resided within the garden; his mother went there every day in person to provide him with food.

After several years had passed in that garden, he contemplated the impurities and defilements of the body’s constituent parts, thinking: "The body is a vessel of suffering; what use is there for this?"
He then relinquished his body and life, entering into *nirvāṇa* and passing away.
His mother immediately performed the funeral rites (*yañña*), erected a stūpa, and made offerings of flowers and incense.
At another time, the king came to this garden; seeing the stūpa, he asked those around him:
"Now, there has never been such a stupa in this garden; who has erected it?
The mother of the Pratyekabuddha then replied, "It is the youngest among the king’s princes."
Seeing the king as he emerged, he asked me,
"What great king is this, so majestic and sublime?
I immediately replied:
“Sudariśānti, the Wheel-Turning Sage King, is your father.
He then asked me again, “When shall I become king?”
I said to him, "Among your thousand sons, you are the youngest; you should not receive the kingship. His son then spoke:
"If he were not permitted to become a king, what would be the use of him remaining at home as a layman?
He then took leave of me to go forth and study the Path, and I granted his request.
I made a pact with him:
"If you attain the Way, you must certainly return to see me.
He shaved off his beard and hair, donned the kāṣāya, and went into the mountains and marshes to practice meditation with diligence, thereby attaining the path of a pratyekabuddha.
In accordance with his vow, he returned and saw me.
I immediately invited him to stay within this garden, providing him daily with all necessary food, drink, and requisites.
After several years had passed, he entered parinirvāṇa; we performed the funeral rites here and erected a stūpa and temple.
"This is that very stupa.
Upon hearing these words, the king was both moved by grief and filled with joy; he replied to the lady, "Why did you not tell me?"
"I would have bestowed upon him the rank of a Wheel-Turning King; it would not have been right for me to hear such a great loss.
Now, even though he is dead, I shall bestow the kingship upon him."

He immediately removed his celestial crown and the royal regalia adorned with the seven treasures, placing them atop the stupa; he then held a great royal parasol made of the seven treasures over the stupa and prostrated himself before it, making offerings of flowers and incense and providing entertainment with music.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"In times past, that King Śuddhodana-Śāṇa, the Wheel-Turning Monarch, was none other than my own self.

At that time, I made offerings to the stūpa of my son who had become a Pratyekabuddha; I bestowed upon him the royal throne and placed a great parasol of the seven precious jewels over the stūpa. By virtue of this merit, for incalculable kalpas I have been a Wheel-Turning Monarch, ruling over the four continents, with the seven treasures following me, and three thousand seven-jeweled parasols constantly arriving of their own accord."
Throughout incalculable kalpas, whether as the Lord of Devas or as the Brahma King, up until this very day,
had I not attained Buddhahood, these three thousand precious canopies would have continued to arrive spontaneously and without end.

Making offerings to a single stūpa of a pratyekabuddha brings forth merit that is inexhaustible; how much more so for those who make offerings to the physical body of a Tathāgata, or who, after his parinirvāṇa, erect stūpas for his relics or fashion images of the Buddha to worship them? When one calculates their merit, it surpasses the former by hundreds of thousands of billions of times, by incalculable multiples, beyond all comparison.

At that time, the great assembly was filled with immense joy; their minds were delighted and their understanding was resolved. Simultaneously, there were those who attained the fruit of *srotāpanna*, *sakṛdāgāmin*, *anāgāmin*, or *arhat*; some gave rise to the aspiration for unsurpassed, perfect, and true enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*); and others established themselves in the stage of non-retrogression—all beyond measure or calculation.
At that time, the great assembly was filled with immense joy; they circumambulated the Buddha three times, prostrated themselves with their heads at his feet, and each returned to their own place.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One proceeded to the city of Vaiśālī, and upon reaching the threshold of the gate, he spoke these verses:
"The various devas dwelling on earth, And the various devas residing in space..."
All you who have come here, you should all give rise to a heart of loving-kindness.
Day and night, harbor joy; you should follow the words of the True Dharma.
Do not harbor harmful intentions, nor cause affliction and distress to the people.
