At that time, when the Tathāgata spoke these words of true and subtle truth,
all the pestilence-demons fled toward the kingdom of Magadha, and the illnesses in the kingdom of Vaiśālī were entirely cured.
At that time, the Buddha returned once more to the kingdom of Magadha, while the pestilence spirits returned to the kingdom of Vaiśālī.
During this period, the World-Honored One traveled back and forth seven times, and he then spoke these words:

"Since countless kalpas past, I have cultivated meritorious deeds and made great vows; now, by means of this true and correct practice, I shall eliminate all physical ailments of sentient beings as well as their mental afflictions."
The Buddha said:
"When I was King Śibi, for the sake of a single pigeon, I cut the flesh from my own body and made a vow to eliminate all dangers for every sentient being."
When he was the Prince Mahāsattva, he relinquished his body and life for the sake of a starving tigress.
When he was King Śibi, he personally offered his own flesh to nourish a sick man for twelve years.
During the time of King Amitodgalaya, he was ill and prepared medicine himself intending to take it.

At that time, there was a Pratyekabuddha who was also ill; coming together with the king, he begged for medicine. The king, though not taking it himself, immediately took the medicine and gave it to the Pratyekabuddha, making a vow that all illnesses might be completely cured.

During the reign of King Śuddhodana, he saved the lives of one hundred kings who were facing death; he led King Kāśyapa of Kamboja to enter into right view, and caused the evil oaths of twelve years to be dissolved.
When he was Prince Sudāna, he gave away his two children and his wife as alms.

When he was Prince Mahiṃsaka, he used medicine to eliminate the illnesses of sentient beings, and further, having entered the great ocean, he obtained *maṇi* jewels to relieve the poverty of sentient beings.
When King Mahāpāli was ill, for twenty-four days he offered his own flesh to provide for the sick.
When the rishi Kṣāntivāda was being dismembered, having his hands and feet cut off, he did not give rise to a single thought of anger.

During the reign of the King of Kāśī, the people suffered from a pestilence. The king observed the eightfold precepts of the fast and gave rise to a heart of great compassion, directing his thoughts toward all sentient beings; consequently, those among the people who were ill were all completely cured.

When Vibhūṣaṇa served as a master of incantations, there was an epidemic among the people; he used his own flesh and blood to perform the exorcism, giving it for the demons to devour, and thus all the many illnesses of the people were completely cured.
In the time of King Brahmā, for the sake of a single verse, he flayed his own skin to write the sutra.
In the time of King Vilepanīya, for the sake of a single verse, he drove a thousand nails into his body.
In the time of the seer Udraka, for the sake of a single verse, he flayed his own skin to serve as paper, broke his bones to serve as a pen, and used his blood to mix with ink.

In the time of King Bandhumat, all the people within the kingdom suffered from ulcerous diseases. The king went out himself and saw a poisonous tree; when its leaves fell into the water, those who drank that water became ill. He immediately uprooted the poisonous tree, including its roots and stumps, and burned them all with fire, whereby half of the people’s ulcerous diseases were cured.
Among them, some remained incurable.
The king asked the physicians,
"Why do the sores and illnesses of these sentient beings fail to heal?"
The physician replied to the king, "This wound is severe; it can only be cured by eating fish and meat.
Upon hearing these words, the king went immediately to the water's edge, climbed a tree, and made a vow to become a fish.

"Now, with this body, I shall eliminate the illnesses of sentient beings; I take these merits to seek the Buddha-way, universally removing the immeasurable physical and mental illnesses of all sentient beings."
"If it be truly as I wish, may the illnesses of all sentient beings who eat my flesh be completely cured.
He then threw himself from the tree into the water, whereupon he was transformed into a fish and spoke with a voice, saying:
"May those who have illnesses come and take my flesh to eat; their ailments shall be cured."
When the people heard the sound, they all came to take the fish and meat and eat them, and their illnesses were entirely cured.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One spoke of his own accord:
"The karmic actions performed in previous lives and the vows I made have now all been fulfilled."
"Now, by means of this true and correct teaching, I shall eliminate all calamities and misfortunes for all sentient beings.

At that time, the Buddha manifested himself with two heads; one head looked toward the kingdom of Vaiśālī and the other looked toward the kingdom of Magadha. The pestilence demons were all driven away back to the great ocean, and the many diseases of the people were entirely cured.

The five grains ripened in abundance and the people lived in peace and happiness; he transformed them extensively through the Dharma, causing all the maladies of desire within their minds to become completely purified, establishing them upon the Path, so that all the people were filled with great joy.
Thereupon, the bhikṣus praised with one voice:
"The Tathāgata’s immeasurable merits are most marvelous, most extraordinary, and inconceivable.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"Not only have I now removed the afflictions of sickness, hunger, and thirst for the multitude of beings, but it was also thus in past ages.

In the distant past, countless eons ago, there was a great king of this Jambudvīpa named Brahmā, who ruled over eighty-four thousand minor kings of Jambudvīpa. He had twenty thousand consorts and ten thousand court ladies, yet he had no crown prince."

Day and night she was filled with sorrow and anxiety, offering prayers and sacrifices to the spirits and deities—the Brahmā heavens and the Śakra-devānām-indra, the great gods such as Mahābali, and the sun, moon, earth, and heaven—whereupon she finally obtained a son.
At that time, the sons born were all handsome and exceptionally fine, possessing the marks of a great man;

they were named Mahesvara. They were compassionate and benevolent, intelligent and wise. Regarding the world’s classics, the movements of the stars and constellations, and the eclipses of the sun and moon, there was no technical skill with which they were not thoroughly proficient. Furthermore, they studied the art of medicine and the compounding of various drugs, proclaiming throughout the kingdom:
"All those who are ill should come to me; I shall provide them with medicine, food and drink, and attend to their care."

When the people heard this decree, all those who were ill went to the Prince; everyone in the kingdom, both great and small, was filled with joy and did not fail to praise his virtue. They no longer sought out other physicians nor treated them with contempt.
Consequently, all the other physicians became filled with anger and envy toward the Prince.

"At that time, throughout Jambudvīpa, pestilence broke out among the people and grain prices rose even higher; though all available medicines were gathered, they could not cure them, and those who died among the populace increased greatly day by day."
The King was deeply grieved and anxious, and he issued a command to summon all the physicians to inquire about their prescriptions and medicines.
At that time, there was a physician who harbored envy toward the Prince; he thought to himself:
"This Prince is now my enemy, and I have finally found an opportunity."
He then said to the king, "There is yet another method; let us exhaust all means to search for it, and Your Majesty may then proceed accordingly.
He departed immediately and returned the following day, whereupon he addressed the king again:
"Having identified one remedy, if Your Majesty were to take it, all your ailments would surely be eliminated.
The king then said, "What medicine is required? Speak of it at once."
The physician replied to the king:

"One must obtain the blood of someone who, from birth, has been compassionate and merciful toward sentient beings and has never given rise to a thought of anger; this blood should be mixed with medicine and administered. Furthermore, one must obtain both of his eyes to drive away the spirit, and only then will all the illnesses be cured."
The king immediately replied:
"Since birth, I have never given rise to anger; this is truly rare.
This matter is extremely difficult and cannot be achieved."
Upon hearing this, the Prince said to his father the King:
"This matter is easy; it is not difficult to accomplish.
Thus the Prince spoke to the King.

"I am the son of the King, my father; since birth, I have never harbored anger or malice toward others, and I have always been compassionate toward all beings, never manifesting even the slightest sign of ill-will."
"My body is impermanent and lacks solidity; before long, it too shall surely die.
I only pray that Your Majesty will grant me permission to act as medicine to eliminate the illnesses of the multitude."
The king then replied: "I have no offspring;
I prayed to and sacrificed to the various heavens, the sun, the moon, the stars, and the four mountains and five peaks, and thereby I obtained this son."
"I would rather lose my life and kingdom now than ever listen to you.
The Prince then addressed his father, the King, saying:
"I seek the Way of the Buddha; I shall now give my own blood to sentient beings, and by means of this merit, I shall fully understand all the sūtras and teachings of the Buddhas."
I now bestow these physical eyes upon sentient beings; by this merit, may I attain the wisdom-eye of a Tathāgata and act as a true guide for all.
"Great King, although you have no crown prince, you are nevertheless able to be king;
yet if the realm were devoid of people, for whom would you be king?
May all the ailments of the people be entirely removed, and may our father the king also be free from sorrow."
The king wept again and replied to the prince, saying:
"Now I would rather abandon my royal throne than truly forsake my pitiable son.
Thereupon, the prince knelt upright with palms joined and addressed his father, the king, saying:
"Now that I seek the unsurpassed, truly correct path, if I were to cherish this foul and impure body, how could I attain the profound and wondrous Dharma of the Tathāgata’s wisdom?"
"How may I attain the all-encompassing eye of wisdom?
I only pray that my father, the King, will not cause me to turn back from this unsurpassed resolve for the Way.
The father king remained silent and said nothing further.
The physician said to the king:
"I shall first take some blood and mix it with medicine to give to the patients; if they recover, I will then extract my eyes, but if they do not recover, there is no need to extract them."
Thereupon, the Prince pricked his arm and drew blood, making this vow:

"By means of this blood, I shall eliminate the illnesses of all sentient beings. I dedicate this merit toward the attainment of unsurpassed, true, and perfect enlightenment; if I truly become a Buddha, then for all sentient beings who take this medicine, their illnesses shall be cured."
He then mixed the medicine with his own blood and gave it to the various patients; their illnesses were all cured.
The physician then addressed the king:
"All those who have taken this medicine have been completely healed. You may believe this by observing the manifest facts before your eyes."

At that time, the eighty-four thousand minor kings, subjects, and citizens of Jambudvīpa, hearing that the Great King’s crown prince had personally gouged out his own eyes to compassionately save all beings, were moved to tears; they all gathered together, knelt with palms joined, and addressed the crown prince, saying:
"We pray only this, O Crown Prince of the Great King!"
"We would rather ourselves surrender our own lives than allow the Prince to have his eyes destroyed.
Since you show such compassion for all sentient beings, you will soon attain Buddhahood; we pray that you do not destroy your own eyes."
Thereupon, the Prince admonished and took leave of the kings, ministers, and citizens, saying:
"I shall now use these eyes of flesh and blood to eliminate the illnesses of sentient beings; I shall take this merit and employ it to seek the Way of the Buddha."
"When I attain Buddhahood, I shall eliminate both your physical ailments and your mental afflictions; do not cause me to retreat from my unsurpassed resolve for the Way.
At that time, all the kings, ministers, and subjects, having heard these words, remained silent.
Thereupon the Prince commanded his attendants:
"Prepare the instruments for extraction; I wish to pluck out his eyes.
He spoke thus to those around him:
"Who is able to pluck out my eyes?
The people on his left and right all declined, saying they were unable.
At that time, a physician who harbored envy toward the prince replied:
"I can," [the man replied]. The Prince was delighted and said in response, "Excellent!"
He took up a knife and handed it to him, saying to the physician,
"Pry out an eye and place it in my palm.
The physician then pried out one eye and placed it in the Prince's palm.
Thereupon, the Prince made this solemn vow:

"Now I give these fleshly eyes of mine to sentient beings; I do not seek the status of a Wheel-Turning Sage King, nor that of a Mara King, nor that of a Brahma King, nor the pleasures of form, sound, fragrance, flavor, or touch. I take this merit to seek the unsurpassed, right, and true Way, so that I may attain the eye of all-knowledge and universally act as a Great Physician-King for immeasurable sentient beings throughout the ten directions, removing all physical and mental illnesses of sentient beings and bestowing upon them the eye of wisdom."
Having spoken these words, he immediately placed his eyes upon the table, saying:
"If it is truly as my heart's wish, may the illnesses of all sentient beings be completely healed."
Upon seeing this, his parents immediately fainted, regaining consciousness only after a long time;

the kings, ministers, and citizens raised their voices in wailing, shaking heaven and earth as they rolled on the ground and threw themselves down, some even falling into a state of bewildered unconsciousness.

Just as he was about to raise his knife to gouge out the other eye, at that very moment, the great trichiliocosm shook violently. The devas of the three realms all descended, seeing that for the sake of sentient beings the Bodhisattva had gouged out his own eye and blood flowed forth; countless devas wept with such grief that their tears fell like torrential rain.
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, approached the Prince and asked him:
"Out of compassion for sentient beings, you now disregard your own body and life to extract your physical eyes; such diligent suffering is truly most difficult."
What do you seek with these meritorious deeds?
Do you seek to become a wheel-turning monarch, a lord of the gods, a Mara king, or a Brahma god?
What vow does the prince seek to fulfill?
The Prince replied:

"I do not seek the status of a holy king, a celestial lord, a Mara king, or a Brahma king; nor do I seek the pleasures of the three realms—the delights of form, sound, fragrance, taste, and touch. I shall take these merits to seek the unsurpassed, true, and correct path, acting as a great physician-king for all sentient beings of the ten directions to universally eliminate the physical and mental illnesses of all beings, bestowing upon them the eye of wisdom so that they may be forever free from all the afflictions of birth and death."
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, and all the devas praised him, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!
How truly marvelous and unsurpassed!"
"As you have wished, you shall attain Buddhahood before long.

Then, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, took his own eye and restored it to the Prince's eye; at that moment, the Prince’s eye was completely healed, becoming even more brilliant and beautiful than it had been before.
Immeasurable devas immediately scattered heavenly flowers upon him, all of them filled with joy.
The father king, as well as the mother, the queen, the court ladies, and all the kings, ministers, and subjects, were all greatly delighted and leaped for joy beyond measure.
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, commanded the Great General Vemacitrin to drive away all pestilential spirits back to the great ocean, so that all those who were ill were completely healed.

The Heavenly Lord then rained down various kinds of food and drink; next, he rained down grains and rice; next, he rained down clothing; and next, he rained down the seven treasures. The illnesses of all sentient beings were completely cured, and everyone was fully satiated with no one left hungry or thirsty. The people rejoiced, and the kingdom subsequently flourished.

After several years, his father the King passed away, and he ascended the throne. As he sat upon the main hall, the seven treasures appeared spontaneously; he became a Wheel-Turning King ruling over the four continents, such that none failed to receive his blessings, and the merit he had cultivated was realized in this very life.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"The Crown Prince Mahādeva at that time was none other than myself.
The Father King Brahmā at that time was none other than my current father, King Śuddhodana."
The mother at that time was my current mother, Māyā.
The physician who gouged out my eyes at that time was Devadatta.
The people of Jambudvīpa at that time were the people of the kingdoms of Vaiśālī and Magadha now.

At that time, I also removed their afflictions of sickness, hunger, and thirst; now, I likewise eliminate the physical and mental illnesses of sentient beings, enabling them all to attain the eye of wisdom and be established in the realization of the Path.
"When a bodhisattva practices the perfection of giving, their diligent toil is such as this.
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had said, all the bhikṣus were greatly rejoiced and paid homage to the Buddha.
Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, together with one thousand two hundred and fifty bhikṣus. He intended to enter the city for alms.

When that Buddha was about to enter the city, five hundred devas first released a fragrant wind that blew upon the roads and through the alleys, making them all pure; impurities, filth, excrement, and foul-smelling places naturally sank into the earth, leaving the roads entirely clean and pristine.
Five hundred devas and humans rained down fragrant essences, moistening all the roads and streets, while scattering celestial flowers.

When the king, his ministers, and the people beheld this auspicious omen, they knew that the Buddha was about to arrive; they all abandoned their cherished affairs and duties, and rushed forth to welcome the World-Honored One.

When the people saw the Buddha, among them were some who swept the ground, some who scattered flowers, some who burned incense, and some who spread their robes upon the ground. Among them were those who loosened their hair and spread it on the ground, wishing for the Buddha to step upon it as he passed; those who threw themselves prostrate on the ground, spreading their bodies in the four directions so that the Buddha might tread upon them; those who held banners and parasols; and those who performed music. With single-minded devotion and palms joined, they gazed at the Buddha with pure intent.
All sentient beings each paid various forms of reverence to the World-Honored One.
At that time, there was a certain brahmin who was so impoverished that he lacked flowers and incense for offerings and felt deeply ashamed of himself.
He thought, "I have no other recourse; I must simply focus my mind and purify my intent as I gaze upon the Buddha."
Thereupon, with profound reverence and a heart full of exultation, he stood with palms joined, gazing upon the Tathāgata, and praised the Buddha in verse, speaking these stanzas:
“Your countenance shines like refined gold, The thirty-two marks are radiant;
Among all classes of sentient beings, None who behold you fail to rejoice.”
"Beholding the Buddha, my heart leaps with joy; all sorrow and grief are utterly dispelled.
Having forever crossed the ocean of birth and death, I bow my head in homage to the Great Peace.

At that time, the World-Honored One smiled with delight, and five-colored rays of light issued from his mouth in a thousand and ten hundred wondrous forms. From each ray of light emerged countless luminosities, and at the tip of every ray was a lotus flower made of the seven treasures. Upon each flower sat a transformation Buddha, illuminating the ten directions.

From the great hells below up to the Heaven of the Thirty-three above, he illuminated everywhere the dark and obscure places of the five realms of existence; throughout the entire sphere of the Buddha, there was no place that was not brilliantly lit. Among the devas and humans of the trichiliocosm, all who beheld the Buddha’s radiance leaped for joy; each abandoned their palaces and left behind their pleasures, and all came together to where the Buddha was.

There are those who attain liberation upon hearing the Dharma of the sutras; those who attain liberation upon seeing its radiance; those who attain liberation upon hearing the Dharma preached by transformation Buddhas; and those who attain liberation by following the light to the presence of the Buddha.
All those in immeasurable hells undergoing torture and punishment shall find complete rest, and after their lives end, they shall all be reborn in the heavens.

Among all the animals and beasts, a virtuous mind will spontaneously arise; they will face one another with compassion and refrain from harming each other, and after their lives end, they too shall be reborn in the heavens.

Among the hungry ghosts, all spontaneously obtained food of a hundred flavors; they were free from any thought of hunger or thirst, leaping for joy with no further sense of stinginess, and after their lives ended, they were all reborn in the heavens.

Immeasurable sentient beings—those who were blind gained sight; those who were deaf gained hearing; those who were mute were able to speak; those with hunched backs were able to straighten; those who were bound or crippled were able to walk; all their various ailments and infirmities were completely healed; and all those imprisoned and confined were fully released.

At that time, among the devas and humans of the great trichiliocosm, there was no one in the entire assembly who did not rejoice; their minds were all purified, free from the three defilements. Among them, some attained rebirth in the heavens, some attained the fruit of stream-entry, some the fruit of once-returning, some the fruit of non-returning, some attained arhatship, and some attained the path of the pratyekabuddha. Some resolved to attain unsurpassed, perfect, and true enlightenment, while others firmly established themselves in the stage of non-retrogression—each such instance being beyond measure or calculation.
After the World-Honored One’s radiance had illuminated the ten directions, it returned, circled his body three times, and entered through the space between his eyebrows.
Thereupon, Ānanda adjusted his robes, knelt with palms joined, and stepped forward to address the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, this present smile must surely have a cause; I only pray that you will explain it."
The Buddha said to Ānanda,
“Do you see this brāhmaṇa? Ānanda replied:
“Yes, I have seen it.
The Buddha told Ānanda:

“Because this brāhmaṇa praised the Buddha with a single verse of pure mind, from this time forward for thirteen kalpas, he shall receive natural rewards among devas and humans; he will always be handsome, eloquent, and possessed of wisdom, praised by all people, and never fall into the three evil realms or the eight difficult conditions. Hereafter, he shall all become pratyekabuddhas, named ‘Joyful.’”
When the entire assembly heard what the Buddha had spoken, they were all filled with joy and sang praises of the Buddha’s virtues.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying,
“The merits of the Tathāgata are inconceivable.”
“The merit obtained by this brahmin from praising the Buddha with this single verse is immeasurable; how truly wonderful it is!
The Buddha told Ānanda:
“It is not only today that this brahmin has praised me and thereby gained such wholesome benefit.”
In the distant past, there was a king of Vārāṇasī named Brahmadatta who went out on a hunting expedition, escorted before and behind by elephant troops, cavalry, and chariot forces.
While hunting in the mountains, he found a white elephant whose body was as white as snow, lovely in its luster, and possessed six tusks.
Upon obtaining this elephant, the king was filled with great joy and immediately entrusted it to a mahout to be trained.
At that time, the elephant trainer immediately placed a collar upon him, fastened him with a yoke and a tether, and confined him with a heavy staff.
Thereupon, the elephant wept with tears falling; for seven days he refused to eat or drink.
The elephant trainer was terrified and anxious, thinking, "This is the king's elephant; if it does not eat or drink, it will die before long.
He then addressed the king, saying:
"The white elephant we have obtained refuses to eat or drink, and it weeps with tears falling.
Upon hearing these words, the king went immediately to see it.
The king asked the elephant:
"Why do you not eat?
The elephant then spoke in human speech and addressed the king, saying:
"My heart is filled with sorrow; I only pray that Your Majesty will remove my grief."
The king asked again,
"What kind of sorrow is there?
The elephant replied to the king:
"I have parents who are aged and infirm, unable to walk about; as there is no one else to provide for them, I alone support them by gathering food and drink."
If I remain here bound and receive no offerings, we shall both perish; for this reason, I am filled with grief and sorrow.
Great King, if you possess great compassion, [please grant me my life].
"Release me so that I may go and provide for my parents until the end of their lives; I shall surely return to serve Your Majesty and will not break this vow.
Upon hearing these words, the king was moved with sorrow and displeasure, and he immediately praised him, saying:
"Though you are an animal, you practice the conduct of a human; though I am a human, I act like an animal."
The king then knelt down for a long time, released the elephant, and let it go.
At that moment, the elephant departed; it remained in service to its parents for twelve years, and when they passed away, it immediately returned to the royal palace.
When the king saw the elephant return, his joy increased all the more; he adorned its body with ornaments made of the seven treasures.

As the king was about to depart, the elephant led the way before him. The king’s love for this elephant surpassed that for his crown prince, as it was the most excellent among all the elephants; therefore, it was named Elephant Banner (Hastidhvaja).
At that time, there was a poor brāhmaṇa who wished to go to the king to beg for alms, and he asked people, saying:
"By what means can one obtain wealth? Someone said to him:
"The King has a white elephant that he holds very dear; if you can praise this elephant, you shall receive a great reward.
At that time, the brahmin waited for the king to go out and stood by the roadside. He then praised the white elephant, speaking these verses:
"Your body is most beautiful, Like the elephant of the Lord of Devas."
The multitude of elephants possess all auspicious marks; their merit is most sublime and lofty.
Their form and shadow have no equal, like the radiance of white snow.
Their bodies are exceedingly difficult to match; they are marvelous and immeasurable.
At that time, when the king heard the praise of the white elephant, he was greatly delighted and bestowed five hundred gold coins upon the brahmin, by which he became wealthy.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"At that time, the one with the elephant-banner was none other than myself.
The brahmin at that time is this very brahmin here now."
At that time, they praised me and thereby gained benefit, using it to relieve their poverty and want.

Now that I have attained Buddhahood, they praise me once again; the merit and reward they obtain will be immeasurable, and by means of this, they shall be delivered from the perils of birth and death.
Ānanda knelt with his right knee on the ground and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"If there were someone who praised the Tathāgata with a single four-line verse, how much karmic reward of merit would they obtain?"
The Buddha told Ānanda:

"Suppose hundreds of thousands of millions of nayutas of countless sentient beings were all to attain human bodies and each achieve the path of a pratyekabuddha; and suppose someone were to provide these pratyekabuddhas with offerings of clothing, food and drink, medicine, bedding, and mats for a full hundred years—would the merit of that person not be great?"
Ānanda said to the Buddha, “It is exceedingly much, exceedingly much; it is beyond measure.

“The Buddha replied, ‘If there were someone who, with a heart of joy, praised the Tathāgata with even a single four-line verse, the merit they would obtain would exceed that of one who obtains the blessings from making offerings to all the pratyekabuddhas by hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of times, countless times over—there is no way to compare them.’”

The venerable Ānanda and the entire great assembly, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, were all greatly rejoiced; they circumambulated the Buddha three times and prostrated themselves, touching their heads to his feet in salutation.
Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying in a monastery in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī.

It is the nature of all Buddhas that, three times during the day and three times during the night, they survey sentient beings with the eye of perfect awakening; whoever is ready for deliverance, they immediately go to deliver them.
At that time, the King of Vārāṇasī had a brahmin minister who had recently taken a wife whom he cherished and respected deeply.
His wife said to her husband,
"Grant me one wish."
The minister replied,
"Whatever you wish to seek, do as you please.
The wife then answered:
"Listen as I offer alms to the Buddha and the community of bhikṣus; I shall serve them with my own hands and you may listen to the preaching of the Dharma.
The husband then approved, saying: "Do as you wish."
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing that they were ready for deliverance, rose early the following morning, donned his robes, took up his bowl, and went to their home.

Hearing that the Buddha was outside, the minister and his wife were filled with joy and leaped for gladness; they immediately went out to welcome him, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, prepared a seat, invited him to enter and sit, and offered him sweet delicacies.
When the World-Honored One had finished his meal, the prime minister and his wife personally took up water and poured it over the hands of the World-Honored One.

Thereupon, after the Tathāgata had washed his hands and rinsed his mouth, he preached the Dharma for them, praising the virtue of giving and the merit of observing the precepts, [explaining] how one receives natural rewards among devas and humans—honorable, illustrious, noble, wealthy, and enjoying infinite bliss.
Though one may be of high station and indulge freely in all desires, one cannot escape the sufferings of the three miserable realms.

Within the hells, there is burning by fire and boiling in cauldrons; there are mountains of knives and trees of swords, chariots of fire and furnaces of glowing coals. Being dismembered and sawn apart with blades and saws is most cruel and agonizing, beyond full description. As for the suffering among the hungry ghosts, their bodies are emaciated while their bellies are vast and their throats are as narrow as the eye of a needle. Their bones and joints strike and grind against one another, and their entire bodies blaze with fire. For hundreds of thousands of myriads of years, they do not hear the names of water or grain; their hunger and thirst are so extreme that they cannot be fully described.

Among the animals, there is suffering: tigers, wolves, lions, snakes, pythons, vipers, and adders prey upon and devour one another. Within these three miserable realms, malevolence burns fiercely; there is not a single thought of kindness even as large as a hair. They wallow in bitter poison with no prospect of escape.
Only by relinquishing all desires and contemplating the True Realities can one escape the manifold poisons of suffering.

To receive a body within the three realms is entirely suffering; all such sufferings arise from habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*). Through the habitual pursuit of desires and the defilements of the three poisons, the retribution of various formations (*saṃskāra*) gives rise to manifold sufferings.

By severing the three poisons and extinguishing all desires, there are no further formative activities (*saṃskāra*); when all activities are exhausted, one no longer receives a body; and when there is no body, all sufferings are extinguished.
"Those who wish to exhaust all conditioned phenomena and every bond should contemplate only the Eightfold Noble Path.

After the Buddha had explained this Dharma to the minister and his wife, at that moment, the husband and wife were filled with joy and leaped for gladness as they entered into the Four Noble Truths; they immediately attained the stage of Srotāpanna before the Buddha.

Thereupon, the husband and wife viewed their home as a prison and saw desire as fire; finding no joy in affectionate attachment, they knelt long upon their knees and addressed the Buddha, saying, "We wish to become śramaṇas."
The Buddha granted his consent.

Their hair and beards fell away of their own accord, and the dharma robes appeared upon their bodies; the husband immediately became a śramaṇa and the wife became a bhikṣuṇī, and they both followed behind the Buddha to the vihāra.
At that time, the World-Honored One again preached the Dharma for them, concerning the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment and the various dhyānas and samādhis.
Through contemplation and understanding, their desires were forever extinguished, and they all became arhats with the six supernormal powers clearly manifest.
At that time, the bhikṣus praised the Tathāgata’s supernormal powers and wisdom, and further extolled the two arhats:
"How extraordinary and marvelous!
To be able to renounce noble status and honorable wealth while still in one's prime, and for his wife to likewise abandon desire and pleasure in her youth—this is truly difficult to equal."
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"This arhat, in his previous lives as well, possessed a virtuous mind, and now his intention remains virtuous.

In the past, immeasurable eons ago, there was a king named Brahmadatta in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī. The king had a minister named Vidura, who was compassionate and benevolent, intelligent and widely learned, with no field of knowledge in which he was not proficient. He taught and transformed others solely through the ten wholesome paths of action; neither the king nor his subjects failed to seek his counsel and receive his instruction, for the king held him in great respect and affection."
At that time, there was a sea dragon king named Pāruṇi, who had a queen named Manasā whom he deeply loved and revered.

When the dragon king wished to go to the heavens to join the assembly at the abode of Śakra, he entrusted his wife to five hundred court ladies within the palace, instructing them: "You must not disturb or provoke her, nor cause her mind to be troubled."

After the Dragon King had departed, the lady sat and reflected upon the events of her past lives. Recalling her former existence as a human being, she remembered how she had violated the precepts and thereby fallen among the dragons; immediately, she became despondent and wept, shedding tears.
Seeing that she was unhappy, the female attendants all asked her together:
"Why are you unhappy? The lady replied:

"I recall that in a previous life when I was originally a human being, I sat and transgressed the prohibitions and precepts; thus, I have now become a dragon and must endure this poisonous, evil, and loathsome form.
Because of this, I find no joy."
He asked his attendants:
"By what means can I escape this dragon body and be reborn in the heavens?
The attendants replied:
"Because one possesses the form of a dragon with such fierce and blazing venom, it is extremely difficult, indeed most difficult, to seek liberation from this dragon body and be born in the heavens!
Even seeking a human body is still unattainable, let alone being born in the heavens."
Among them, one woman replied:

"I have heard that in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī in Jambudvīpa, King Brahmadatta has a minister who is exceedingly compassionate and benevolent, whose wisdom is peerless, and who has mastered all the scriptures. He knows the destinies of all beings within the five realms of rebirth among gods and humans, and he teaches and transforms others through the five precepts and the ten wholesome paths of action."
"If you can go and question him, you will then know the practices for being born in heaven and the conduct for escaping the state of a dragon.
When the Dragon King returned, he saw that the lady's countenance was unhappy, so he immediately asked her,
"Why are you not happy?"
The lady replied:

"In the kingdom of Vārāṇasī in Jambudvīpa, there is a king named Brahmadatta who has a minister called Viduḷa. He is exceedingly compassionate and merciful toward sentient beings; his wisdom is peerless, and there is no scripture he does not master. I wish to obtain his heart to eat it and his blood to drink it; if I could obtain these, my grief would be dispelled."
The Dragon King replied, "Do not be distressed; I shall seek it out.
Thereupon, the Dragon King had a friend who was a yakṣa named Anañga, to whom he spoke:

"My wife has heard that in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī in Jambudvīpa there is a minister named Viduḥṛta, who is compassionate toward others and foremost in wisdom, with a thorough mastery of all scriptures and treatises; she desires to obtain his heart along with his blood to consume as food, so seek them out for me and bring them here."

He took two bright pearls and gave them to him; thereupon the yakṣa immediately accepted the instruction, took the bright pearls, and departed. Upon reaching Jambudvīpa, he transformed himself into a merchant and entered the city of Vārāṇasī holding the maṇi jewel.
A passerby asked him, "Do you wish to sell this pearl?"
He replied, "I am not selling it; I wish to use it for gambling.
He then immediately informed the king:
"A merchant outside possesses two bright pearls and wishes to use them for gambling.
When the king heard this, he was greatly delighted; relying on his own skill at gambling, he was certain that he would emerge victorious.
The king said,
"Bring him here," and immediately summoned him into the palace.
At that time, the king asked,
"What is your wish? The yakṣa replied:
"If I am victorious, take this vaidūrya and give it to me;
if Your Majesty is victorious, this jewel belongs to the King.
The King agreed to this.
The ministers and attendants all tried to dissuade him.

However, the king was eager for the bright jewel and, relying on his own skill at gambling, thought, "I shall surely win. Disregarding the words of his ministers, he immediately began to gamble with him.
The yakṣa gained the victory and captured Vidūḍabha.
At that time, the yakṣa seized Vidūḍabha and flew straight through the air.
When the king lost Vidūḍabha, he became deeply distressed; all his ministers said:
"A king who practices five things will lose his kingdom and forfeit his position:

first, gambling; second, an addiction to wine; third, indulgence in female beauty and being deluded by music; fourth, a fondness for hunting expeditions; and fifth, failing to heed loyal admonitions."
"If you perform these five things, the King shall not live long.
Thereupon, the yakṣa took Bandhula to the mountains and was about to kill him.
At that time, Vidūra asked the yakṣa,
"Why have you killed me? The yakṣa replied:

"The Dragon King's consort has heard that you are foremost in intelligence and wisdom, and that you are compassionate and benevolent toward others; she wishes to obtain your blood as well as your heart, and for this reason she has killed you."
Pindola said: "Your foolishness prevents you from understanding my intention.
When you heard that I possess wisdom and desired my blood, it was because you wished for my Dharma."
"Those who wish to obtain my heart actually wish to obtain the wisdom within my heart.
Let us go together to see him; whatever he requires, I shall give it all to him."
Then, Pindola immediately spoke to the yakṣa: "There are five things by which a person commits evil: first, acting with haste and lacking careful deliberation;

second, frequently feeling much regret later on; third, harboring much anger and lacking a heart of compassion; fourth, having a bad reputation spread far and wide such that people detest and envy them and do not wish to see them; and fifth, falling after death into the realms of hell, animals, or hungry ghosts."
There are five qualities beloved by those who cultivate goodness. What are these five?
First, they act with careful deliberation;
governing themselves according to the Dharma, they do not act rashly or violently, and thus have no cause for regret later.
Second, he possesses a mind of great compassion and kindness, never inflicting harm upon others;
third, his excellent reputation spreads far and wide, its fame resounding throughout the four quarters;
fourth, all people revere and love him as if he were their own teacher or father.
"Fifth, after death one will be born among the devas or among humans, where happiness shall be boundless.

Thereupon, upon hearing these words, the yakṣa’s mind was immediately opened and liberated; he prostrated with his head at [the teacher's] feet in salutation and requested instruction from Bhadrayaśas.
At that time, Vidūra taught him the Dharma of the ten wholesome actions for rebirth in the heavens.
Having heard the Dharma, the yakṣa rejoiced and leaped for joy, receiving and putting it into practice.

He then led Vidūra to the place of the nāga king. Upon seeing Vidūra, the lady was filled with immeasurable joy; she prostrated herself with her head at his feet, paid homage, and took refuge in him, providing a precious throne and offering a meal of a hundred flavors.
Thereupon, Biduli spoke to the Dragon King and his consort concerning the merits and demerits experienced within the five realms of existence:

"Restrain the three evils of the body; have compassion for all sentient beings and do not inflict harm upon them; abandon stinginess and greed, practicing righteousness and yielding so as not to steal; contemplate the filthiness of desire and remain chaste and pure, free from lust.

Let your speech always be sincere and free from falsehood or deception; let your words always be gentle and devoid of coarse or harsh language; resolve conflicts with harmony rather than litigating between self and others; and let your speech accord with the Dharma, avoiding flowery embellishments."

The mind is always compassionate and patient, never giving rise to anger; seeing others experience joy and goodness, one rejoices on their behalf without a heart of jealousy; with single-minded devotion, one reveres and believes in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha, as well as the true and sublime precepts; clearly understanding both transgression and merit, the mind is free from doubt.
By practicing these ten wholesome actions fully and without deficiency, one will be reborn in heaven, where the palaces of the seven treasures provide all that is desired spontaneously.

By fulfilling five matters—refraining from killing, refraining from stealing, refraining from sexual misconduct, refraining from deception, and abstaining from intoxicants so as not to become drunk—one will be born among humans in the families of kings, great clans, or elders, enjoying honor, nobility, wealth, and pleasure beyond measure.

They lack a heart of compassion and harm sentient beings; they forcibly plunder the wealth of others and commit theft through unrighteous means; they violate the wives of others, never finding satiety in their lustful desires;
they engage in false speech, double-tongued talk, harsh words and abuse, as well as anger and jealousy;
they are unfilial toward their parents, do not believe in the Triple Gem, and turn their backs on the right path to follow what is perverse.
Having committed these various evils, they die and enter hell, where they are scorched, roasted, and flogged; they endure ten thousand poisons and suffer pains beyond description.

Failing to repay debts, failing to return loans, being aggressive and devoid of faith, arrogant and self-important, and slandering the Triple Gem, they fall among the animals upon death. As donkeys, horses, camels, pigs, sheep, dogs, lions, tigers, wolves, vipers, snakes, scorpions, centipedes, lizards, and other such beasts, they prey upon one another; their poisonous minds burn fiercely as they wallow in suffering with no prospect of escape.

Stingy, greedy, and envious, they refuse to practice giving and lack knowledge of proper food and clothing; they do not believe in the Triple Gem and are consumed by the fire of avarice. Upon death, they fall into the realm of hungry ghosts with emaciated bodies, their bones and joints pressed against one another, and their entire forms ablaze with fire. For hundreds of thousands of myriads of years there is no time of release; day and night they suffer from hunger and thirst, never even hearing the names of water or grain.
"Only by practicing the ten wholesome deeds and restraining body, speech, and mind can one long enjoy the infinite bliss of rebirth in heaven.

Thereupon, the Dragon King, his consort, and all the dragons were struck with awe; their hearts trembled and their hair stood on end as they all reverently accepted the ten wholesome deeds, restrained body, speech, and mind, and observed the eightfold fast, whereupon all the dragons rejoiced.
"At that time, when the King of the Golden-Winged Birds (Garuda) desired to come and devour the dragons, he was unable to approach them despite exhausting all his supernatural powers.
Thereupon, the dragons were filled with great joy and marveled at such an unprecedented occurrence."
Dragon Kings, consorts, all the dragons of the great ocean, and all the yakṣas—everyone offered the ten wholesome deeds, none failing to rejoice and pay homage with prostrations.
The Dragon King then asked Pindola:
"Great Master, do you wish to return to Jambudvīpa? He replied:
"I wish to return.
Thereupon, the Dragon King immediately presented the Bodhisattva with sandalwood, mani-jewels, and various exquisite treasures;

the lady, the court ladies, all the dragons, and the yakṣas each offered rare and wonderful rarities. They escorted Pindola back to Vārāṇasī, where they prostrated themselves in worship and departed with joyful hearts.
The various nāgas and yakṣas of the great ocean had their poisonous minds extinguished and all were reborn in the heavens.

King Brahmadatta, along with his ministers and all the people, were able to see the teacher Piṇḍola again; they were all filled with great joy, prostrated themselves at his feet, and inquired after his well-being.
At that time, Vidūṣaka related the beginning and end of these events to the king in full detail.
The king, his ministers, and the common people were all filled with joy and marveled at such an unprecedented occurrence.

Thereupon, Vidūṣaka took the maṇi jewel and placed it atop a banner; with a sincere heart, he made a prayer, and immediately a rain of the seven treasures—robes, food, and drink—fell throughout Jambudvīpa, so that immeasurable ministers and subjects all enjoyed abundance and happiness.

At that time, Śakra, Lord of Devas, together with the human king, the Great Ocean Dragon King, and the Kāla-garuḍa King, each renounced all desires and came to dwell in the mountains and marshes. Observing the fast and practicing seated meditation, they each guarded their own bodies and minds, saying to one another:
"I have obtained much merit."
The Heavenly King spoke of himself, saying:
"I have renounced the pleasures of all the celestial desires; having now come here to restrain my body, speech, and mind, I have attained great merit."
The King of Men spoke again:
"I have renounced all the pleasures of desire within my palace and come here to guard my body, speech, and mind; thus, I shall obtain great merit."
The Dragon King spoke again:
"I have renounced the great ocean, my palaces of the seven treasures, and all the pleasures of desire; now that I have come here to guard my body, speech, and mind, I have gained much merit."
The King of the Golden-Winged Birds also spoke thus:
"This Dragon King is my food; yet, as I now observe the fast and restrain my body, speech, and mind, I have no intent to harm him and do not eat him, whereby I shall gain great merit."
Thereupon, the four kings each sighed, their minds undecided, and said to one another:
"We should now go together to question our teacher, Piṇḍola."
He immediately went to Pindola and, prostrating with his head at [the elder's] feet, each asked him this:
"Who has obtained greater merit?
The Bodhisattva replied:
"You each erect four banners and streamers—blue, white, yellow, and red.
They immediately followed the instruction and erected the four banners and streamers.
The Bodhisattva asked:
"Is its shadow different?
Or is it of one kind of color?
The Four Kings replied:
"The colors of the banners are each different, yet their shadows are of a single color and without distinction.
The Bodhisattva replied,

"When you Four Kings each set aside your desires and come here to maintain the precepts and guard yourselves, the merit you obtain is entirely equal and without difference, just as the shadows of four banners of different colors are of one kind and without distinction."
At that time, the Four Heavenly Kings, having heard his words, each understood their meaning and leaped for joy.
Then, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, immediately offered a celestial karpāsa garment to the Bodhisattva.
At that time, the King of Men immediately presented various exquisite jewels to the Bodhisattva.
The Dragon King of the Great Ocean then took the maṇi-jewel from his topknot and offered it to the Bodhisattva.
The King of the Golden-Winged Birds offered celestial golden ornaments to the Bodhisattva as a tribute.
At that time, the Four Kings were all greatly delighted; they paid their respects and departed.
Then, all the people of Jambudvīpa, along with the nāgas and yakṣas, fully practiced the ten wholesome deeds.
"At that time, all those in the world who reached the end of their lives were reborn in the heavens; none fell into the three miserable realms.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"The state preceptor Vidūḍabha of that time was my very self."
The dragon king Pāruṇi at that time was this current prime minister;
the dragon queen Manasī was this current prime minister’s wife.
In the past, when he was a dragon, he heard the Dharma from me and received it with joy in his heart; he was thus able to cast off his dragon body and be reborn in the heavens.

Now that I have attained Buddhahood, he has heard the Dharma from me and attained liberation through joyful understanding; he immediately left the household life to contemplate wisdom, and having forever exhausted all desires, he has attained Arhatship.
"In past lives his mind was also good, and even up to the present life his mind remains good.
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had said, all the bhikṣus were filled with great joy and paid homage to the Buddha.
The Sutra on the Past Deeds of the Bodhisattva, Scroll Lower.
